[1] RCW 82.04.290: B&O TAX – CLASSIFICATION – SERVICE AND
OTHER ACTIVITES – VOLUME REBATES AND ASSOCIATED SERVICES.
Amounts received as volume rebates, as well as amounts received for performing
services performed to enhance the ability to sell products to third parties, are taxable
under the service and other activities B&O tax classification.
[2] WAC 458-20-254; RCW 82.32.070: B&O TAX – ESTIMATED REBATE
INCOME – ACTUAL REBATE INCOME – RECORDKEEPING. In order to be
able to adjust a taxpayer’s estimated rebate income to reflect their actual rebate
income, a taxpayer has to keep and provide records that show how each of the
taxpayer’s proposed adjustments corresponds from their estimated rebate to the
actual rebate.
[3] WAC 458-20-19402; RCW 82.04.462: B&O TAX – ATTRIBUTION –
REBATE INCOME PRIOR TO 2024 AMENDMENT TO WAC 458-20-19402.
Prior to the 2024 amendment to WAC 458-20-19402, rebate income from sales of
hardware was attributed under WAC 458-20-19402(303)(b), while rebate income
from sales of software was attributed under WAC 458-20-19402(303)(c).
[4] WAC 458-20-228; RCW 82.32.105: PENALTIES – ANNUAL
RECONCILIATION – WAIVER – LACK OF KNOWLEDGE. A taxpayer’s lack
of knowledge that its rebate income is subject to the service and other activities
B&O tax classification and is attributable to Washington is not a circumstance
beyond the taxpayer’s control sufficient to waive penalties assessed.
Fisher, T.R.O. – A technology retailer and wholesaler protests the imposition, classification, and
apportionment of tax on rebate income. The petition is denied. 1
1
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 81
ISSUES
1. Did the Department properly tax rebate payments from manufacturers as being subject to
service & other activities business and occupation (“B&O”) tax classification under RCW
82.04.050 and RCW 82.04.290?
2. Did the Department properly calculate “gross income of the business” under RCW
82.04.080, RCW 82.32.070, and WAC 458-20-254?
3. Did the Department properly apportion rebate income under RCW 82.04.462 and WAC
458-20-19402?
4. May the Department waive penalties and interest under RCW 82.32.105 and WAC 458-
20-228?
FINDINGS OF FACT
. . . (Taxpayer) is a . . . company selling hardware, prewritten software, and maintenance
agreements to businesses, governments, and health care agencies, including in Washington. The
maintenance agreements include the servicing and configuration of the hardware, and providing
IT support. Taxpayer has an office in Washington. In addition to the income Taxpayer receives
from selling hardware, software, and maintenance agreements, Taxpayer receives rebate income
from the suppliers from whom Taxpayer purchases the hardware and software.
Department examined Taxpayer’s books and records to verify Taxpayer’s Washington business
activities and transactions were properly reported on Taxpayer’s excise tax returns between
January 1, 2013, and December 31, 2016 (Audit Period). Taxpayer provided to the Department a
copy of Taxpayer’s general ledger. In comparing Taxpayer’s Washington excise tax returns to
Taxpayer’s general ledger, the Department determined that Taxpayer had been reporting rebate
income under the wholesaling B&O tax classification; the Department reclassified this income to
service & other activities B&O tax classification.
The general ledger included three accounts . . . (collectively, Rebate Estimate Accounts).
Taxpayer’s general ledger recorded the net of the credits and debits in these accounts as the total
amount of rebate income Taxpayer received. The Department determined that the total amount of
credits listed in these accounts, without any deduction of the debits, was the proper amount of
revenue Taxpayer received for rebates.
The Department then apportioned the total rebate income, without deduction of the debits in the
Rebate Estimate Accounts. The Department divided Taxpayer’s total Washington revenue by
Taxpayer’s total revenue for each year of the Audit Period. The Department then multiplied the
resulting percentage for each year by the total rebate income Taxpayer received to apportion the
rebate income taxable in Washington. The Department also assessed service & other activities
B&O tax on unreported income Taxpayer received under its maintenance agreements.

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 82
The Department ultimately assessed Taxpayer $ . . . in service & other activities B&O tax, $ . . .
in interest, and $ . . . in penalties for failing to correct the reporting of the receipts factor for
apportionment for 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016.
Taxpayer timely sought administrative review. Taxpayer does not contest that the rebates are
subject to tax, or the tax assessed on the maintenance agreement revenue.
Taxpayer asserts four arguments. First, Taxpayer asserts that the appropriate B&O tax
classification for rebate income is wholesaling and not service & other activities. Taxpayer argues
that the rebate revenue it receives from suppliers is not in exchange for any services.
Second, Taxpayer asserts that the amounts in the Rebate Estimated Accounts should not be
considered Taxpayer’s gross income. Taxpayer explains that when it makes purchases from
suppliers, Taxpayer estimates the amount of rebate it will receive and records that estimated
amount in its general ledger as a credit. Later, when Taxpayer knows the actual amount of the
rebate, Taxpayer enters a debit in the amount of the estimated rebate and puts in the real amount
of rebate as a credit. According to Taxpayer, the Rebate Estimated Accounts are just the debits
offsetting the estimated rebates when Taxpayer puts the true amount of the rebates, and are
therefore not properly “gross income of the business” under RCW 82.04.080.
Third, Taxpayer disputes the Department’s apportionment methodology. Taxpayer asserts that not
all of its suppliers provide a rebate and that Taxpayer’s revenue includes all customer sales—
including sales that involve products from suppliers that do not provide any rebate. Taxpayer
asserts that this methodology distorts the Taxpayer’s market, and is not a reasonable method of
apportionment. Taxpayer further argues that in determining where the customer receives the
benefit of Taxpayer’s services, the customer is the supplier providing the rebate, and the rebate
income should be apportioned to where the suppliers are.
Fourth, Taxpayer protests the imposition of the penalties for failure to reconcile apportionable
income in the years during the Audit Period. Taxpayer asserts that the penalties and interest should
be waived due to delays in completing the audit. During the audit, the original auditor assigned to
complete the audit was called to active duty military service, and a new auditor was assigned.
Taxpayer declined the Department’s request to sign a waiver of the non-claim period.
Along with its petition for administrative review Taxpayer submitted several documents. Taxpayer
submitted documentation regarding the rebates from Taxpayer’s suppliers. The [Supplier 1] Value
Incentive Program “provides a payment to partners that achieve program objectives during either
a 6-month program period or 3-month program period.” Taxpayer Petition at 26. The program
objectives include requirements to maintain various certifications from [Supplier 1] in addition to
meeting sales volume requirements. Taxpayer Petition at 26-34. [Supplier 2] provides a Marketing
Incentive Fee in exchange for “demonstrating significant achievement of sales in excess of
[Supplier 2]-specified quarterly sales goals.” Taxpayer Petition at 54. In addition, in order to
qualify for the Marketing Incentive Fee a reseller of [Supplier 2] products must be a [Supplier 2]
Certified Reseller or GSA Letter of Supply Holder, [and] must meet [Supplier 2] training
requirements. Taxpayer Petition at 54, 70. Furthermore, half of the Marketing Incentive Fee must
be spent on [Supplier 2] approved marketing and sales enablement activities. Taxpayer Petition at

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 83
81. The Marketing Incentive Fee is payable after the fiscal quarter in which it is earned. Taxpayer
Petition at 55.
Taxpayer submitted a copy of the general ledger account labeled . . . for the 2016 year (“2016
Account Spreadsheet”). The 2016 Account Spreadsheet consists of 100 pages of debits and credits
from 2016. The line description for each item states the name of the rebate. Most of the line
descriptions, but not all, end in the word “reversal” or “accrual.” Each line also has a date. The
2016 Account Spreadsheet is organized by the size of the debit and credit.
Finally, Taxpayer also submitted Exhibits 1 through 38, consisting of 362 pages of line item
amounts. According to Taxpayer, these amounts substantiate the claimed debits in the 2016
Account Spreadsheet. Exhibits 16 through 31 are labeled as being rebates related to 2017 [Supplier
2] Marketing Incentive Fees.
ANALYSIS
Washington imposes a B&O tax for the act or privilege of engaging in business in the state of
Washington. RCW 82.04.220. Taxpayer does not dispute that it has nexus with Washington, and
is, therefore, generally subject to B&O tax in Washington. The B&O tax measure is “the
application of rates against value of products, gross proceeds of sales, or gross income of the
business, as the case may be.” Id. The rate used is determined by the type of activity in which a
taxpayer engages. See generally Chapter 82.04 RCW.
A. B&O Tax Classification of Rebate Income
We first address Taxpayer’s argument that Taxpayer’s rebate income is subject to the wholesaling
B&O tax classification. RCW 82.04.270 imposes wholesaling B&O tax on persons making sales
at wholesale. RCW 82.04.060 defines “sale at wholesale” as, in relevant part, any sale of tangible
personal property which is not a retail sale. RCW 82.04.050(1)(a) defines a retail sale to mean
every sale of tangible personal property to all persons, with six exceptions not relevant to this
determination.
The wholesaling B&O rate is applied against the “gross proceeds of sales.” RCW 82.04.270. RCW
82.04.070 defines “gross proceeds of sales” to mean, in relevant part, the value proceeding or
accruing from the sale of tangible personal property. “Value proceeding or accruing” means the
consideration actually received or accrued. RCW 82.04.090.
Taxpayer receives rebate income for meeting volume requirements and providing other services,
including maintaining certifications and training requirements, in addition to, in the case of the
[Supplier 2] Marketing Incentive Fee, marketing. The suppliers are not paying the rebate in order
to buy tangible personal property from Taxpayer, so the rebate is not consideration accruing from
the sale of a piece of tangible personal property. Because Taxpayer is not selling tangible personal
property to suppliers so the suppliers can resell the tangible personal property, Taxpayer is not
engaged in wholesale sales in exchange for the rebates, and the rebate payments from the suppliers
are not subject to the wholesaling B&O tax classification.

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 84
The suppliers are paying the rebate to induce Taxpayer to keep selling suppliers’ products to third
parties and performing services to enhance Taxpayer’s ability to sell products to third parties. This
is not listed under a specific definition in Ch. 82.04 RCW. Business activities other than, or in
addition to, those that are specifically enumerated elsewhere in Ch. 82.04 RCW or RCW
82.04.290(1) or (3), are taxed under the service and other activities B&O tax classification. [RCW
82.04.290(2) (applying to persons engaged in a business activity “other than or in addition to an
activity taxed explicitly under another section in this chapter or subsection (1) or (3) of this
section”).] Accord [Det.] No. 98-172E, 18 WTD 387, 393-95 (1999) (determining that incentives
from vendors to purchase products are subject to service & other activities B&O tax classification);
[see Steven Klein, Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 183 Wn.2d 889, 897-99, 357 P.3d 59 (2015) (dealer
cash fits within the catchall provision because it is an “other” or “additional” business activity and
not a retail sale).] Because the rebates pay for Taxpayer [activities] that are not specifically
enumerated elsewhere in Ch. 82.04 RCW, the Department appropriately classified the rebates as
service & other activities.
B. Gross Income of the Business and Recordkeeping
We next address Taxpayer’s argument that the Department erred in refusing to net the debits from
the credits listed in the Rebate Estimate Accounts. RCW 82.04.290(2) states that the service &
other activities B&O tax is calculated by applying the relevant tax rate against the “gross income
of the business.” RCW 82.04.080 defines gross income of the business to be “the value proceeding
or accruing by reason of the transaction of the business engaged in.” “Value proceeding or
accruing” means the consideration actually received or accrued. RCW 82.04.090.
Taxpayer asserts that the estimated amounts of the rebate are not amounts “actually received.” We
agree in principle. Gross income of the business includes the value proceeding or accruing by
reason of the transaction of the business engaged in. RCW 82.04.080. Value proceeding or
accruing means the consideration actually received or accrued. RCW 82.04.090. The consideration
actually received or accrued is the amount of the rebate actually received or accrued. According
to Taxpayer, Taxpayer estimates the amount of rebate it will receive for accounting purposes as a
credit, and once Taxpayer receives the rebate and knows the actual amount, Taxpayer then enters
the actual amount of the rebate and debits out the estimated amount. The “value proceeding or
accruing” from the rebate is the amount actually received, not both the amount actually received
and the earlier estimate.
However, we are unable to grant Taxpayer relief. RCW 82.32.070 requires all taxpayers to keep
and preserve suitable records as may be necessary to determine the amount of any tax for which
the taxpayer may be liable. WAC 458-20-254(3) states that all taxpayers have a duty to prepare
and preserve all records in a systematic manner to demonstrate the amounts of gross receipts and
sales from all sources.
The records provided by Taxpayer are insufficient to establish that the debits in the Estimated
Rebate Accounts are adjusting the rebate revenue to reflect the amounts actually received or
accrued without any estimated amounts. The 2016 Account Spreadsheet contains multiple entries
of 2017 [Supplier 2] Marketing Incentive Fees. According to the Marketing Incentive Fee
agreement provided by Taxpayer, Marketing Incentive Fee payments are payable after the end of

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 85
the fiscal quarter in which the Marketing Incentive Fee accrues. It does not follow that the 2016
Account Spreadsheet showing amounts accrued in 2016 would list Marketing Incentive Fees
accrued in 2017.
Furthermore, there appear to be random debits that do not match with credits of a corresponding
amount. For example, on the first page of the 2016 Account Spreadsheet, a line item for “VIP 26
Rebate Reversal” dated for April 30, 2016, is debited for $ . . . . The 2016 Account Spreadsheet is
organized by size, yet there is no credit for the same amount. There are a number of other debit
entries that do not have any corresponding credit entry. If all of the debits in the 2016 Account
Spreadsheet truly represented estimated amounts being canceled out of the general ledger, there
should not be any debit entries that do not have a corresponding credit entry.
In order to establish that the debits are simply adjusting estimated rebate amounts, Taxpayer would
need to show, with records, when Taxpayer put the estimate in the general ledger as a credit, when
Taxpayer received the rebate (and therefore knew the actual amount of the rebate), when Taxpayer
entered in the actual number of the rebate as a credit, and when Taxpayer entered a debit to cancel
the initial estimate for each credit Taxpayer claims should not be included in the measure of gross
income of the business.2
Based on the records before us, we conclude that the Department did not err in refusing to net the
credits and debits of the Estimated Rebate Accounts.
C. Apportionment
RCW 82.04.460 addresses apportionable income in this state and provides:
[A]ny person earning apportionable income taxable under this chapter and also
taxable in another state must, for the purpose of computing tax liability under this
chapter, apportion to this state, in accordance with RCW 82.04.462, that portion of
the person’s apportionable income derived from business activities performed
within this state.
RCW 82.04.460(1). “Apportionable income” is defined as “gross income of the business generated
from engaging in apportionable activities, including income received from apportionable activities
performed outside this state, if the income would be taxable under this chapter if received from
activities in this state . . . .” RCW 82.04.460(4)(a).
“Apportionable activities” include, in relevant part, services and other activities taxed under RCW
82.04.290(2). RCW 82.04.460(4)(a)(vi). As explained above, the rebate income at issue here is
properly classified under the service and other activities B&O tax classification in RCW
82.04.290(2), so it is apportionable income under RCW 82.04.460(1).
2 WAC 458-20-100(6) provides a mechanism for requesting reconsideration of determinations. If Taxpayer has
documentation to establish that it entered estimates of rebate income as credits that were later cancelled out with
debits, Taxpayer should provide such records along with a petition for reconsideration. Taxpayer must comply with
WAC 458-20-100(6) in filing for reconsideration.

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 86
A person’s income within the scope of RCW 82.04.460(1) is apportioned to Washington by
multiplying the person’s apportionable income by the receipts factor. For purposes of computing
the receipts factor, RCW 82.04.462(3)(b) provides that gross income of the business generated
from each apportionable activity is attributable to Washington:
Where the customer received the benefit of the taxpayer's service . . . . When a
customer receives the benefit of the taxpayer's services . . . in [Washington] and
one or more states and the amount of gross income of the business that was received
by the taxpayer in return for the services received . . . can be reasonably determined
by the taxpayer, such amount of gross income must be attributed to [Washington].
RCW 82.04.462(3)(b)(i). “Reasonably determined” in the context of RCW 82.04.462(3)(b)(i)
means “reasonable method of proportionally attributing,” which in turn means a method of
determining where the benefit of an activity is received and where the receipts are attributed that
is “uniform, consistent, and accurately reflects the market, and does not distort the taxpayer's
market.” WAC 458-20-19402(106)(f).
RCW 82.04.462(3)(b)(ii) provides that if the customer receives the benefit of the service in more
than one state and if the taxpayer is unable to attribute gross income under RCW
82.04.462(3)(b)(i), then we attribute gross income of the business where the benefit of the service
was primarily received.
The “benefit of the taxpayer’s service” is not defined in statute. WAC 458-20-19402(303),
however, defines that term in a variety of ways, depending on the factual circumstances:
(b) If the taxpayer’s service relates to tangible personal property, then the benefit is
received where the tangible personal property is located or intended/expected to be
located.
(i) Tangible personal property is generally treated as located where the
place of principal use occurs . . . .
(ii) If the tangible personal property will be created or delivered in the
future, the principal place of use is where it is expected to be used
or delivered.
(iii) The following is a nonexclusive list of services that relate to tangible
personal property:
(A) Designing specific/unique tangible personal property;
(B) Appraisals;
(C) Inspections of the tangible personal property;
(D) Testing of the tangible personal property;
(E) Veterinary services; and
(F) Commission sales of tangible personal property
(c) If the Taxpayer's service does not relate to real or tangible personal property,
the service is provided to a customer engaged in business, and the service relates to
the customer's business activities, then the benefit is received where the customer's

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 87
related business activities occur. The following is a nonexclusive list of business
related services:
(i) Developing a business management plan;
(ii) Commission sales (other than sales of real or tangible personal
property);
(iii) Debt collection services;
(iv) Legal and accounting services not specific to real or tangible
personal property;
(v) Advertising services; and
(vi) Theater presentations
RCW 82.08.010(7) defines “tangible personal property” as “personal property that can be seen,
weighed, measured, felt, or touched, or that is in any other manner perceptible to the senses.” See
also 34 WTD 452 (applying RCW 82.08.010(7) to WAC 458-20-19402(303)(b)).
The services here are meeting volume requirements in selling hardware and software to third
parties, maintaining certifications related to the hardware and software, and marketing the
hardware and software. We analyze the apportionment of rebate revenue related to hardware and
software separately.3
1. The Benefit of Taxpayer’s Service - Hardware Rebate Revenue
The hardware is tangible personal property because it is personal property that can be seen,
weighed, measured, felt, or touched. We conclude that the services of meeting volume
requirements, maintaining certifications related to the hardware sold, and marketing the hardware
are all services that relate to tangible personal property.
Because Taxpayer’s services relate to tangible personal property, Taxpayer’s customers receive
the benefit of Taxpayer’s service either where the tangible personal property’s principal place of
use occurs under WAC 458-20-19402(303)(b)(i) or, “[i]f the tangible personal property will be
created or delivered in the future,” where “it is expected to be used or delivered” under WAC 458-
20-19402(303)(b)(ii). Here, the principal place of use is where the hardware is ultimately delivered
to the end customer. The purpose of the rebates is to get Taxpayer to sell more of the suppliers’
hardware to the end customers.
2. The Benefit of Taxpayer’s Service - Software Rebate Revenue
The suppliers’ related business activity is the production and sale of software. Taxpayer’s service
is the sale of software in volume, maintaining certifications related to the software, and marketing
the software. Because the services do not relate to real property or tangible personal property, and
are provided to the suppliers who are engaged in business, and the services relate to the suppliers’
3 Because it is unclear whether the suppliers offer rebates for the services provided for the hardware and software
differently, we analyze each separately. Even assuming a supplier does not provide separate rebates for hardware and
software respectively, the analysis in the next paragraphs explains that the apportionment would reach the same result.

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 88
business activity, we must apportion to where the related business activity occurs.4 WAC 458-20-
19402(303)(c). The related business activity is getting end customers to use the software. The
purpose of the rebates is to encourage Taxpayer to sell more of the software to the end customers,
to maintain certifications so end customers feel more comfortable purchasing the software
knowing Taxpayer can help them if issues come up, and market the software so that more end
users purchase the software. Accordingly, the benefit of the service is received where the end
customers are who purchase and use the software.
3. The Method of Apportionment of Rebate Revenue
Because the suppliers receive the benefit of Taxpayer’s services as they relate to hardware rebates
and software rebates in more than one state, we must use a reasonable method of proportionally
attributing Taxpayer’s revenue. RCW 82.04.462(3)(b)(i). In determining where the benefit of
Taxpayer’s activity was received, the Department took Taxpayer’s sales sourced to Washington
and divided that number by Taxpayer’s total sales for each year of the Audit Period to calculate a
receipts factor for each year. The Department then took that receipts factor for each year and
multiplied it by the amount of rebate income received each year. This was a reasonable method of
apportionment because the method was uniform, consistent, reflects the market, and does not
distort the Taxpayer’s market. The receipts factor was calculated based on the undisputed
Washington sourced sales divided by the total sales, and was entirely based off of Taxpayer’s own
records.
Taxpayer asserts that this is an unreasonable method of apportionment. According to Taxpayer,
using total revenue includes suppliers that do not offer any rebate amounts, and so using total
revenue to calculate receipts distorts the Taxpayer’s market. We disagree. The amount of revenue
derived from sales of products from suppliers that do not offer rebates as compared to sales of
products from suppliers that do offer rebates are presumably the same for both Washington sourced
sales and total sales. Indeed, Taxpayer has offered no reason why the comparative amounts would
not be the same for both the national sales and Washington sales. Therefore, any distortion
resulting from the inclusion of revenue from suppliers who do not offer rebates would be on both
the numerator and denominator of the receipts factor, thereby cancelling each other out.
Accordingly, we reject Taxpayer’s argument that this method of apportionment distorts its market.
D. Penalties
Finally, Taxpayer requests waiver of the penalties and interest due to how long the Department
took to issue the audit.
Taxpayer was assessed penalties under RCW 82.04.462(4) for failure to correct the reporting of
the receipts factor for apportionment for 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016. Taxpayer was also assessed
interest on these amounts pursuant to RCW 82.04.462(4).
The Department is an administrative agency, and its authority to waive or cancel penalties is
restricted to the authority granted by the Legislature. The Legislature has granted the Department
4 Even if we determined that software was tangible personal property, the benefit of the service would still be received
where the end customers of the software are located, as explained in the previous section.

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 89
limited authority to waive or cancel penalties. RCW 82.32.105 and RCW 82.32A.020. The
Department has no discretionary authority to waive or cancel penalties. Det. No. 98-85, 17 WTD
417 (1998); Det. No. 99-285, 19 WTD 492 (2000).
The only authority to cancel penalties is found at RCW 82.32.105, which provides:
(1) If the department of revenue finds that the payment by a taxpayer of a tax less
than that properly due or the failure of a taxpayer to pay any tax by the due date
was the result of circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer, the department
of revenue shall waive or cancel any penalties imposed under this chapter with
respect to such tax.
(2) The department shall waive or cancel the penalty imposed under RCW
82.32.090(1) when the circumstances under which the delinquency occurred do not
qualify for waiver or cancellation under subsection (1) of this section if:
(a) The taxpayer requests the waiver for a tax return required to be filed under RCW
82.32.045, 82.14B.061, 82.23B.020, 82.27.060, 82.29A.050, or 84.33.086; and
(b) The taxpayer has timely filed and remitted payment on all tax returns due for
that tax program for a period of twenty-four months immediately preceding the
period covered by the return for which the waiver is being requested.
RCW 82.32.105(2)(a), (b). In sum, all penalties may be cancelled if it is found that the penalty was
caused by a circumstance beyond the control of the taxpayer. Waiving a penalty based on the
Taxpayer not having paid a tax return late during the prior 24 months only applies to delinquent-
payment penalties.
WAC 458-20-228 explains that “[c]ircumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer are generally
those which are immediate, unexpected, or in the nature of an emergency. Such circumstances
result in the taxpayer not having reasonable time or opportunity to obtain an extension of the due
date or otherwise timely file and pay.” WAC 458-20-228(9)(a)(ii). The circumstances must
directly cause the late payment or substantial underpayment. WAC 458-20-228(9)(a)(i).
WAC 458-20-228(9)(a)(ii) lists examples of circumstances that are beyond a taxpayer’s control
sufficient to cancel penalties:
• Erroneous written information from the Department;
• An act of fraud or conversion by the taxpayer’s employee or contract helper which the
taxpayer could not immediately detect or prevent;
• Emergency circumstances around the time of the due date, such as the death or serious
illness of the taxpayer or a family member or accountant; or
WAC 458-20-228(9)(a)(iii) also lists examples of situations that are generally not beyond the
control of a taxpayer:

Det. No. 21-0036, 45 WTD 080 (June 9, 2026) 90
• Financial hardship;
• A misunderstanding or lack of knowledge of a tax liability; or
• Mistakes or misconduct on the part of employees or other persons contracted with the
taxpayer.
Here, Taxpayer requests waiver because of the length of the audit. This is not a circumstance
beyond the Taxpayer’s control, because the length of the audit was not the cause of the late
payment as required by WAC 458-20-228(9)(a)(i). Taxpayer incurred penalties because it did not
file an annual reconciliation to correct its apportionment receipts factor for each year of the Audit
Period. The last year of the Audit Period was 2016, and the corrected receipts factor was due
October 31, 2017. The Audit taking until 2019 to complete was not the cause of the penalty.
Taxpayer’s lack of knowledge that its rebate revenue was subject to service & other activities B&O
tax, was apportionable, and required Taxpayer to file corrections to its receipt factor in each year
of the Audit Period was the cause of the penalties.
Next we turn to RCW 82.32.105(2)(b), which allows the Department to waive penalties when a
taxpayer has timely filed and paid all tax returns due in the twenty four months prior to the penalty.
The earliest penalty during the Audit Period was assessed based on the failure to file a corrected
receipts factor for the 2013 tax year. Taxpayer did not timely file a corrected receipts factor for the
2012 tax year. Accordingly, Taxpayer does not qualify for waiver of taxes under RCW
82.32.105(2)(b).
Finally, we turn to interest. RCW 82.32.105(3) provides that the Department may only waive
interest if the failure to timely pay the tax was the direct result of written instructions given to the
Taxpayer by the Department or if the extension of a due date for payment of an assessment was
not at the request of the taxpayer and was for the sole convenience of the Department. Here, the
failure to timely pay the tax was not the direct result of any written instructions from the
Department; Taxpayer does not allege any such instructions exist. Furthermore, there was no
extension of a due date; Taxpayer was given a due date, and promptly filed a petition for
administrative review. Accordingly, the Department cannot waive interest.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
. . .
Dated this 17th day of February 2021.

RCW 82.04.650; B&O TAX – EXEMPTIONS – INVESTMENT CONDUITS
AND SECURITIZATION ENTITIES. A taxpayer seeking exemption as a
securitization entity has not established that it was directly formed by a bank
holding company; absent such a showing, the Department properly declined to
consider the additional criteria required for the exemption.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
McCormick, T.R.O. – A group of grantor’s trusts that were formed by the subsidiary of a bank
holding company disputes the Department’s tax assessment because the group asserts it qualifies
for the securitization entity exemption from business and occupation (B&O) tax. Because the
group has not established that it was formed by a bank holding company, we deny the petition.1
ISSUE
Whether, under RCW 82.04.650, members of a group of grantor’s trusts that were formed by the
subsidiary of a bank holding company qualify as securitization entities and are therefore exempt
from B&O tax.
FINDINGS OF FACT
[Trust 1], [Trust 2], and [Trust 3] (collectively, Taxpayer) are grantor’s trusts formed by . . .
(Corporation). The purpose of the trusts is to issue and sell notes receivables. Taxpayer earns
interest income on student loans from borrowers in various states, including Washington.
Corporation was formed as a subsidiary of [Bank], which operates as a bank.2 [Bank] is a
subsidiary of [Financial Services Corporation] and is not a bank holding company under 12 U.S.C.
§ 1841. In 2010, . . . acquired ownership of Corporation and Taxpayer. Corporation provides
private student loans to pay for college and graduate school. Taxpayer as “[t]he issuing entity is a
. . . statutory trust created under a trust agreement dated as of December 8, 2006. . . . [Taxpayer’s
1
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.
2 . . .

Det. No. 22-0198, 45 WTD 104 (June 9, 2026) 105
only activities are that it acquires, owns, and manages the trust loans and other trust assets.
Taxpayer also issues payments on the notes and enters into swap agreements, under which it makes
payments, and other related activities.]” Taxpayer Final Offering Memorandum at 5.
While conducting a review of Corporation’s business activities, the Department’s Audit Division
(Audit) discovered that Corporation reported income Taxpayer received on Corporation’s excise
tax returns. As a result, Audit conducted a review of Taxpayer’s business activities for the period
of January 1, 2016, through December 31, 2019. Throughout the review period, Taxpayer was not
registered with the Department. All of the Taxpayer trusts are considered disregarded entities for
federal income tax purposes. However, because each separate entity is taxable in Washington,
Audit credited Corporation for Taxpayer’s income it reported, registered Taxpayer with the
Department, and issued notices of balance due (Assessments) to Taxpayer.3 The Assessments
remain unpaid.
Taxpayer petitioned for administrative review of the Assessments. Taxpayer asserts Audit
incorrectly issued the Assessments because Taxpayer is a qualifying securitization entity and is
exempt from B&O tax. Taxpayer asserts that Audit incorrectly interprets the statutory requirement
of being formed by a bank holding company as requiring a qualifying securitization entity to be
directly formed by a bank holding company. Taxpayer asserts that because it was formed by
Corporation, which was a subsidiary of a bank holding company, it satisfies the statutory
requirement. Taxpayer argues, “The formation structure and purpose is consistent with the
meaning of securitization entity, an entity used as a conduit holding discreet pool of credit, i.e.
student loans. . . . The receivables are transferred to [Taxpayer] as collateral for the trust
securities.” Petition at 5. Taxpayer asserts that because it was formed by a bank holding company
and satisfies the additional requirements to qualify for the exemption, Taxpayer’s income qualifies
for the securitization entity exemption.
In support of its petition, Taxpayer submitted a Prospectus Supplement to Prospectus for each of
Taxpayer’s entities and a Participant List for [Trust 2] listing . . . as the only investor.4
ANALYSIS
Washington’s B&O tax is imposed on every person “for the act or privilege of engaging in business
activities” and applies to the gross income of the business. RCW 82.04.220. “Business” for B&O
tax purposes includes “all activities engaged in with the object of gain, benefit, or advantage to the
taxpayer or to another person or class, directly or indirectly.” RCW 82.04.140. “Gross income of
the business” is broadly defined and means:
[T]he value proceeding or accruing by reason of the transaction of the business
engaged in and includes gross proceeds of sales, compensation for the rendition of
3 [Letter 1], issued October 7, 2021, includes $. . . in service and other activities B&O tax, $. . . in unregistered business
penalty, $. . . in delinquent penalty, and $. . . in interest. [Letter 2], issued October 5, 2021, includes $. . . in service
and other activities B&O tax, $. . . in unregistered business penalty, $. . . in delinquent penalty, and $. . . in interest.
[Letter 3], issued on September 30, 2021, includes $. . . in service and other activities B&O tax and $. . . in interest.
4 Taxpayer did not provide a participant list for either [Trust 1] or [Trust 3], stating the information was not readily
available.

Det. No. 22-0198, 45 WTD 104 (June 9, 2026) 106
services, gains realized from trading in stocks, bonds, or other evidences of
indebtedness, interest, discount, rents, royalties, fees, commissions, dividends, and
other emoluments however designated, all without any deduction on account of the
cost of tangible property sold, the cost of materials used, labor costs, interest,
discount, delivery costs, taxes, or any other expense whatsoever paid or accrued
and without any deduction on account of losses.
RCW 82.04.080. The phrase “value proceeding or accruing” is defined as “the consideration,
whether money, credits, rights, or other property expressed in terms of money, actually received
or accrued.” RCW 82.04.090. Under this broad definition, a service provider may not deduct any
of its costs of doing business from its gross income. See Pilcher v. Dep’t of Revenue, 112 Wn.
App. 428, 49 P.3d 947 (2002) (citing Rho Co. Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 113 Wn.2d 561, 570, 782
P.2d 986 (1989)). Thus, unless a specific exemption, deduction, or exclusion applies, all of
Taxpayer’s gross income is subject to B&O tax without any deduction for overhead or other
expenses. The Legislature “intended to impose the business and occupation tax upon virtually all
business activities carried on within the state.” Simpson Inv. Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 141 Wn.2d
139, 149, 3 P.3d 741 (2000) (quoting Time Oil Co. v. State, 79 Wn.2d 143, 146, 483 P.2d 628
(1971)).
Here, Taxpayer received income during the review period, which was reported on Corporation’s
excise tax returns. Thus, Taxpayer’s gross income is subject to B&O tax unless a specific
exemption applies. Taxpayer asserts that the income it received qualifies for the securitization
entity exemption under RCW 82.04.650.
RCW 82.04.650 relevantly provides:
Exemptions – Investment conduits and securitization entities.
(1) This chapter does not apply to amounts received by . . . securitization
entities from cash and securities.
(2) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
. . .
(c) “Securitization entity” means an entity created by a bank holding
company if the entity created:
(i) Has no employees;
(ii) Has no direct profit-making motive;
(iii) Owns no tangible assets, other than cash, fixed or revolving discrete
pools of credit or charge card receivable originated by a financial institution,
or securities;
(iv) Acts solely as a conduit, allocating its income to holders of its
ownership interest; and
(v) Has as its sole business activities the:
(A) Acquisition of such discrete pools of credit or charge card receivables;
and
(B) Issuance or causing the issuance of securities primarily to persons not
affiliated with the entity.

Det. No. 22-0198, 45 WTD 104 (June 9, 2026) 107
(d) “Bank holding company” has the same meaning as provided in the bank
holding company act of 1956, as existing on June 1, 2010, or such
subsequent date as may be provided by the department by rule, consistent
with the purposes of this section.
. . .
(Bold in original, italics ours.) Thus, to qualify for the securitization entity exemption, the entity
must first have been created by a bank holding company, then satisfy all of the additional statutory
requirements.
The Bank Holding Company Act of 1956 is found in 12 U.S.C. § 1841, et seq. The version of 12
U.S.C. § 1841 that was in effect on June 1, 2010, relevantly provides:
(a)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (5) of this subsection, “bank holding
company” means any company which has control over any bank or over any
company that is or becomes a bank holding company by virtue of this chapter.
(2) Any company has control over a bank or over any company if—
(A) the company directly or indirectly or acting through one or more other
persons owns, controls, or has power to vote 25 per centum or more of any class
of voting securities of the bank or company;
(B) the company controls in any manner the election of a majority of the
directors or trustees of the bank or company; or
(C) the Board determines, after notice and opportunity for hearing, that the
company directly or indirectly exercises a controlling influence over the
management or policies of the bank or company.
. . .
12 U.S.C. § 1841 (effective October 13, 2006, through July 21, 2020) (bold in original, italics
ours).
Here, Taxpayer was formed by Corporation, which was a subsidiary of a bank holding company.
Taxpayer asserts that because a bank holding company formed Corporation which then formed
Taxpayer, Taxpayer meets the statutory requirement of having been created by a bank holding
company. Taxpayer opines Audit’s interpretation of the requirement for Taxpayer to have been
directly formed by a bank holding company in order to qualify for the exemption is incorrect. We
disagree.
The plain language of RCW 82.04.650 requires that a qualifying “securitization entity” be created
by a bank holding company. RCW 82.04.650(2)(c). The term “‘bank holding company’ means any
company which has control over any bank or over any company that is or becomes a bank holding
company.” 12 U.S.C. § 1841(a)(1) (2006). The statutory requirements for the securitization entity
exemption are clear. In order to qualify for the exemption, Taxpayer must first establish that it was
created by a company that has control over any bank or bank holding company. Only after an entity

Det. No. 22-0198, 45 WTD 104 (June 9, 2026) 108
establishes it was formed by a bank holding company must we consider whether each of the
additional criteria are satisfied.
Taxpayer does not assert and has provided no records that establish Corporation has control over
any bank or any company that is or becomes a bank holding company. Thus, we are unable to
conclude Corporation is a bank holding company for purposes of the exemption. Because
Taxpayer has not established that it was formed by a bank holding company, we need not consider
whether the additional required criteria under RCW 82.04.650(c)(i)-(v) have been met. We deny
the petition.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer’s petition is denied.

Tax Credit program for the 2022 tax year, arguing the Department incorrectly removed two
qualifying children from Applicant’s application. We deny the petition.1
ISSUES
1. Under RCW 82.08.0206 and WAC 458-20-285, does an individual meet the eligibility
requirements for the Working Families Tax Credit [(WFTC)] when another party
previously claimed the same two qualifying children for the same tax year?
2. Whether an individual is entitled to a penalty waiver under RCW 82.32.105 and WAC 458-

FINDINGS OF FACT
. . . (Applicant) is an individual residing in Washington. On April 14, 2023, the Department
received Applicant’s WFTC application for the 2022 tax year (Tax Year). In the application,
Applicant reported earned income of $ . . . for the Tax Year and claimed two qualifying children.
On May 8, 2023, the Department’s automated system approved Applicant’s WFTC application for
the Tax Year and issued Applicant a refund of $ . . . . After Applicant received the refund, the
Department’s WFTC Division manually reviewed the application and determined that they needed
more information to confirm that Applicant was, in fact, entitled to the refund [they] already
received. On June 13, 2023, the Department sent Applicant a request for more information related
to the residency of the two qualifying children [they] claimed because another party had claimed
the same children on a separate WFTC application . . . . On June 14, 2023, the Department also
sent Applicant a request for a copy of Applicant’s 2022 federal income tax return with a copy of
the schedule EIC . . . .
On September 13, 2023, the Department sent a Notice of Balance Due in the amount of $. . . with
a due date of March 13, 2024, to Applicant after a manual review showed the qualifying children
were also claimed by the children’s other parent. . . . The Department reviewed a parenting plan
showing proof of residency and guardianship provided on the other parent’s WFTC application
and determined that the other parent was the custodial parent for the purposes of the [Earned
Income Tax Credit] (EITC) and removed them from Applicant’s account. Based on that
documentation, the Department determined that Applicant and the children’s other parent ceased
to live in the same place on December 1, 2022, and on December 2, 2022, the children resided
with the children’s other parent the remaining days of the Tax Year. The Department then reduced
Applicant’s WFTC from $ . . . to $ . . . due to the removal of the qualifying children.
On October 27, 2023, a second Notice of Balance due was issued showing a balance due of $ . . .
and a due date of March 13, 2024, . . . . On December 1, 2023, the Department sent Applicant a
notice stating their application had been denied due to a failure to provide the additional
information requested . . . .
On March 1, 2024, Applicant provided a copy of their 2022 tax transcript. On March 15, 2024, the
Department issued a third Notice of Balance Due in the amount of $. . . showing an increased
WFTC overpayment of $. . . , an assessment penalty in the amount of $. . . , and interest in the
amount of $. . . due to the rejection of Applicant’s application on December 1, 2024, and
Applicant’s failure to pay the assessment before the due date. . . . . On March 27, 2024, the
Department determined that Applicant had excluded their self-employment income from their
WFTC application and added $. . . of self-employment income with a $. . . tax deduction, bringing
their total income for the Tax Year to $ . . . .
On May 22, 2024, Applicant submitted a Petition for Review. Applicant argues in their petition,
“both Mom & Dad claimed kids, when children lived with both Mom & Dad[.] Dad paid all
medical, childcare, and name was on home lease. Copies of proof turned in already.” Taxpayer’s
Petition, pg. 3. Applicant did not request a hearing on their petition.

P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 24-0266, 45 WTD 118 (June 9, 2026) 120
On June 14, 2024, the Department sent a request for additional information as Applicant’s Petition
for Review did not include any additional documentation to support Taxpayer’s arguments. . . .
The Department stated in the request, “to preserve our jurisdiction over your petition for review
we will accept the document dated May 21, 2024, as timely filed. However, a petition for review
must comply with WAC 458-20-100, which requires an adequate statement of facts and reasons
for the review and documents supporting the [applicant’s] position. Such information is necessary
in order for us to better evaluate your case.” Id. Applicant did not respond to this request for more
information and the Department was unable to make contact [with] Applicant.
ANALYSIS
1. Eligibility for Working Families Tax Credit
The WFTC is a tax credit provided to eligible low-income persons in the form of a refund of retail
sales and use taxes paid after January 1, 2022. RCW 82.08.0206(1). The Department calculates an
applicant’s WFTC refund amount based on the applicant’s “properly filed federal income tax
return for the period for which [the applicant is] claiming the refund.” WAC 458-20-285 (“Rule
285”), Answer 10C.
The definition of an “eligible low-income person” is composed of five elements. See generally
RCW 82.08.0206; Rule 285, Part 1.
1. The individual must have a valid Social Security number (“SSN”) or Individual Taxpayer
Identification number (“ITIN”). Rule 285(1)(a).
2. The individual must have properly filed a federal income tax return for the prior federal tax
year. RCW 82.08.0206(2)(a)(i)(B); Rule 285(1)(b).
3. The individual generally must be eligible for the federal EITC provided in Title 26 U.S.C.
Sec. 32 of the Internal Revenue Code, “including meeting the federal income thresholds,”
regardless of whether the individual actually claimed or received the EITC.2 RCW
82.08.0206(2)(a)(1)(A); Rule 285(1)(c).
4. The individual must have been a Washington resident during the year for which the
individual claims the WFTC. Rule 285(1)(d).
5. The individual must have paid Washington sales or use tax on taxable purchases made
during the tax year for which the individual claims the refund. Rule 285(1)(e).
Here, the primary element of this dispute is whether Applicant meets the federal income thresholds
to be eligible for the EITC. Specifically, the issue before us is whether Applicant’s two children
are “qualifying children” under the rules of the EITC. As such, this analysis will primarily address
that element.
To qualify for the EITC, an applicant’s income “must be below the federal adjusted gross income
(AGI) threshold . . . .” Rule 285(4). If the applicant’s AGI is “at or above the federal income
threshold, [the applicant is] not eligible for the EITC” and, therefore, ineligible for the WFTC.
2 An individual will meet this element if the individual or the individual’s spouse or qualifying children “have a valid ITIN instead
of a SSN, which is not permitted under federal EITC eligibility requirements.” Rule 285(1)(c).
Administrative Review & Hearings Division
P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 24-0266, 45 WTD 118 (June 9, 2026) 121
Rule 285(4). The AGI threshold for a single person with no qualifying children for the Tax Year
is $16,480 while the AGI threshold for a single person with two qualifying children is $49,399. ..
Rule 285, Answer 10(E).
Here, Applicant’s earned income as initially reported on their WFTC application was $. . . , which
was below both limits. However, the Department later determined that Applicant’s income was,
in fact, $. . . after analyzing Applicant’s federal tax transcript for the Tax Year. This increase puts
Applicant’s income over the threshold for a single person with no qualifying children. Applicant
has made no argument that the Department incorrectly increased Applicant’s income for the Tax
Year. Thus, Applicant will only qualify for the EITC, and consequently, the WFTC, if they are
able to claim their children as qualifying children. As such, our analysis now turns to whether
Applicant may claim these two children as qualifying children for the purposes of the EITC and
WFTC.
In situations where several people could potentially claim the same qualifying child, the
Department must use the following hierarchy of “tie breaker” rules set forth in Rule 285 to
determine who can claim the child:
(a) If only one person is the child’s legal parent (“parent”): The parent may claim
the child;
(b) If both parents file a joint tax return with each other: They may claim the child;
(c) If both parents claim the child on separate tax returns: The parent with whom
the child lived with the longest during the year may claim the child;
(d) If the child lived with each parent for the same amount of time: The parent with
the higher AGI for the year may claim the child;
(e) If neither parent can claim the child: The person who had the highest AGI for
the year may claim the child; and
(f) If a parent can claim the child but does not: The person who had the highest AGI
for the year may claim the child, but only if that person’s AGI is greater than the
AGI of any of the child’s parents who can claim the child.
Rule 285, Answer 10H (emphasis added). See also IRS Publication 596, Rule 9.
Here, Rule 285, Answer 10(H)(a) and (b) do not apply to the Applicant’s situation. Applicant
argues that the two children lived with both parents during the tax year and that Applicant paid for
all medical care, childcare, and was the name on the lease where the children lived. However, the
Rule 285 tiebreaker rules must be strictly applied, and the analysis must only focus on who the
children lived with the most days during the Tax Year.

P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 24-0266, 45 WTD 118 (June 9, 2026) 122
The other parent provided documentation with their own WFTC application that showed that the
two parents lived together from January 1, 2022, until December 1, 2022. The other parent then
had primary custody of the two children from December 2, 2022, to December 31, 2022. Applicant
has provided no documentation to refute the documentation provided by the other parent. Thus,
the two children lived with the other parent longer during the Tax Year and the Department
correctly determined the other parent was the custodial parent for purposes of the EITC and WFTC.
Therefore, Applicant was unable to claim the two children as qualifying children, Applicant did
not meet the federal income threshold to be eligible for the EITC to qualify for the WFTC, and the
Department properly issued an assessment for the full refunded amount.
2. Penalty Waiver
Taxpayers have certain rights and responsibilities under Washington law, including the
responsibility to file accurate returns and pay their taxes in a timely manner. Ch. 82.32A RCW. In
the event the Department determines that a taxpayer has paid less tax than was properly due, the
Department “shall assess against the taxpayer such additional amount found to be due.” RCW
82.32.050(1).
Whenever the Department issues an assessment for unpaid taxes, it must also include interest. Id.
Interest is calculated from the last day of the month following the final period assessed. WAC 458-
20-228(7). Upon receiving payment from a taxpayer, the Department must apply the payment to
interest and penalties first, then to tax, without regard to any direction from the taxpayer. RCW
82.32.080(5)(a).
If a taxpayer fails to pay an assessment by the due date, the Department must assess an assessment
penalty of 15 percent of the taxes due. RCW 82.32.090(2). The assessment penalty will increase
to a total of 25 percent of the taxes due if the taxpayer does not submit payment to the Department
by the 30th day following the assessment’s due date. Id.
The Department must impose interest and penalties when the conditions for imposing them are
met. RCW 82.32.090(1); Det. No. 01-193, 21 WTD 264 (2002); Det. No. 99-279, 20 WTD 149
(2001).
Here, Applicant does not argue that the penalties or interest were improperly assessed by the
Department, only that they were entitled to the WFTC. As previously determined, Applicant was
not eligible for the WFTC. Thus, the Department properly issued the assessment against Applicant
and Applicant failed to pay the assessment or request a Petition for Review before the due date of
the assessment. Therefore, the Department properly imposed the penalties and interest[] on the
assessment.
In closing, if Applicant made a mistake on their WFTC application, they could file an amended
application. Applicant can visit our website for more information at workingfamiliescredit.wa.gov,
or contact our call center during business hours at 360-763-7300.

information.

We deny the petition.

RCW 82.08.986; RCW 82.12.986: SALES TAX EXEMPTION – USE TAX
EXEMPTION – DATA CENTER EXEMPTION – CERTIFICATE –
EMPLOYMENT REQUIREMENTS – QUALIFYING EMPLOYEE. Among
other requirements, in order to receive the sales and use tax exemption for
purchases using a data center tax exemption certificate, taxpayers must meet certain
employment requirements, including creating a certain number of new permanent
employment positions. In order to be a “new permanent employment position”
under RCW 82.08.986(3)(c), the statute requires that the position not exist or not

and wage minimums and other criteria within the six-year statutory period.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
LaMarche, T.R.O. – A taxpayer that operates a data center in Washington State disputes the
disallowance of certain sales and use tax exemptions it claimed under its data center tax exemption
certificate. The Department disallowed the exemptions on the basis that the taxpayer did not meet
certain employment requirements in the six-year period after it acquired the certificate. We deny
the petition.1
ISSUE
Has Taxpayer shown that it met the employment requirements to qualify for the sales and use tax
exemptions in RCW 82.08.986 and RCW 82.12.986, respectively, on its purchases of tangible

ANALYSIS
RCW 82.08.020 imposes a tax on retail sales in this state. Under RCW 82.04.050(1), the term
“retail sale” includes sales of tangible personal property, and such sales are subject to sales tax,
unless an exclusion or exemption applies. Washington imposes retail sales tax on each retail sale
in this state unless an exemption applies. RCW 82.08.020. “Retail sale” also includes “the sale of
or charge made for tangible personal property consumed and/or for labor and services rendered in
respect to . . . [t]he constructing, repairing, decorating, or improving of new or existing buildings
or other structures under, upon, or above real property of or for consumers.” RCW 82.04.050(2)(b).
RCW 82.12.020 complements the sales tax and, in relevant part, imposes a use tax on the privilege
of using within this state as a consumer, any article of tangible personal property or retail service
for which sales tax legally due has not been paid by the present user.
In 2010, the Legislature adopted certain tax exemptions related to the construction and operation
of data centers, and the purchase of certain eligible server equipment and related labor and services
needed to install that equipment. The Legislature explained its reasons for the exemptions, stating
in relevant part, “It is the legislature's intent to encourage immediate investments in technology
facilities that can provide an economic stimulus, sustain long-term jobs that provide living wages,
and help build the digital infrastructure that can enable the state to be competitive for additional
technology investment and jobs.” Laws of 2010, 1st sp. sess., ch. 1, § 1 (emphasis added).
The new sales tax exemptions were codified in RWC 82.08.986, and use tax exemptions were
codified in RCW 82.12.986, which indicate taxpayers qualify for the use tax exemptions only if
they have qualified for and received a data center exemption certificate pursuant to RCW
82.08.986.2 For simplicity, because the disputed employment requirements for the data center
exemptions for sales tax and use tax are identical, in our discussion we will focus on the sales tax
provisions in RCW 82.08.986, with the understanding that qualification under RCW 82.08.986
implies qualification under RCW 82.12.986.
RCW 82.08.9863 provides a retail sales tax exemption “for sales to qualifying businesses and to
qualifying tenants of eligible server equipment to be installed, without intervening use, in an
eligible computer data center, and to charges made for labor and services rendered in respect to
installing eligible server equipment. . . .” RCW 82.08.986(1).
2 Sales tax provisions were adopted under Laws of 2010, 1st spec. sess., ch. 1, § 2. Use tax provisions were adopted
under Laws of 2010, 1st spec. sess., ch.1, § 3.
3 In our discussion, we will refer to the relevant language in the most recent version of RCW 82.08.986. Other than
minor changes not material here, it is the same language adopted in Laws of 2010, 1st spec. sess., ch. 23, § 1601, which
revised the original language adopted earlier the same year (see Laws of 2010, 1st spec. sess., ch. 1, § 2) to expand on
the employment requirements for qualifying businesses. In 2012, Laws of 2012, 2nd spec. sess., ch. 6, § 302 modified

space. In 2015, Laws of 2015, 3rd spec. sess., ch. 6, § 302 added provisions pertaining to facilities for which

There is no dispute that Taxpayer used the Exemption Certificate to make certain purchases
without payment of retail sales tax. The issue here is whether Taxpayer met certain employment
requirements under the statute to qualify for the data center sales and use tax exemptions.
We note that tax exemptions are construed narrowly, and taxpayers bear the burden of proof when
claiming a tax exemption. In general, “[t]axation is the rule and exemption is the exception.”
Budget Rent–A–Car v. Dep’t of Rev., 81 Wn.2d 171, 174, 500 P.2d 764 (1972). “The taxpayer has
the burden of establishing eligibility for an exemption.” Stroh Brewing Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue,
104 Wn. App. 235, 240, 15 P .3d 692 (2001). Thus, Taxpayer has the burden of showing that it
qualifies for the data center exemption.

based only on the space occupied by the qualifying tenant in the eligible computer
data center.
(Emphasis added.) Thus, as indicated above, because Taxpayer leased approximately . . . square

six “family wage employment positions.” Id.
RCW 82.08.986(3)(c)(i) defines “family wage employment positions” as:
[N]ew permanent employment positions requiring forty hours of weekly work, or their
equivalent, on a full-time basis at the eligible computer data center and receiving a wage
equivalent to or greater than one hundred fifty percent of the per capita personal income of

purposes of this subsection (3)(c), “new permanent employment position” means an
employment position that did not exist or that had not previously been filled as of the date
4 We note that Taxpayer has made arguments that certain independent contractors should be counted in its total of new

that the department issued an exemption certificate to the owner or qualifying tenant of an
eligible computer data center, as the case may be. . . .
(Emphasis added.)

Employee A
The goal of statutory interpretation is to carry out the intent of the legislature. Lake v. Woodcreek
Homeowners Ass’n, 169 Wn.2d 516, 526, 243 P.3d 1283 (2010). Statutory interpretation begins
with the statute’s plain meaning. Id. “The ‘plain meaning’ of a statutory provision is to be discerned
from the ordinary meaning of the language at issue, as well as from the context of the statute in
which that provision is found, related provisions, and the statutory scheme as a whole.” State v.
Jacobs, 154 Wn.2d 596, 600, 115 P.3d 281 (2005) (citing Wash. Pub. Ports Ass’n v. Dep’t of
Revenue, 148 Wn.2d 637, 645, 62 P.3d 462 (2003); Dep’t of Ecology v. Campbell & Gwinn, LLC,
146 Wn.2d 1, 10-11, 43 P.3d 4 (2002)).
Here, the statute is clear on its face when it defines a “new permanent employment position” as
“an employment position that did not exist or that had not previously been filled as of the date that
the department issued an exemption certificate.” RCW 82.08.986(3)(c) (emphasis added).
Taxpayer indicates in its May 2019 Memo that prior to the issuance of the Exemption Certificate,
it intended to create a permanent position for Employee A to fill. Specifically, Taxpayer says that
in the early fall of 2010, prior to . . . [the Exemption Certificate issue date], “[Employee A] was
dual-hatted at this time: He was charged with running a [. . .] data center facility . . . [out-of-state]
while also bearing the responsibility of visiting [Washington] as [Taxpayer’s] lead data center
engineer to be eventually assigned to [the Data Center’s location in Washington].” May 2019
Memo, at 1 [(emphasis added)]. Also, Taxpayer’s employee portal indicates that Employee A was
associated with [the Data Center’s location in Washington] . . . [prior to the Exemption Certificate
issue date].5
. . . .
Therefore, Employee A’s position was not one “that did not exist or that had not previously been
filled as of the date that the department issued an exemption certificate.” RCW 82.08.986(3)(c).
As such, Employee A’s position does not qualify under the plain language of the statute, and cannot
be included in the calculation under RCW 82.08.986(3)(a) and (b) of net employment for any of
the years, 2010 through 2016.
5 Taxpayer argues that Employee A’s tax withholdings were changed from . . . [out-of-state] to Washington on . . . ,
three days after the Exemption Certificate was issued, which it argues means that Employee A became a permanent
employee after the certificate’s issue date. However, although reflective of a payroll change, it does not indicate
whether the job itself was “permanent” in the sense in which this term is used in RCW 82.08.986(3)(c).

Det. No. 20-0129, 45 WTD 071 (June 9, 2026) 78
Taxpayer argues that no positions, including Employee A’s, could have been new “permanent”
employment positions prior to the date it entered into a lease with the building owner,6 or received
a certificate of occupancy, both of which it says occurred after the Exemption Certificate was
issued, because there was no certain place in which the employees could work.
However, the word “permanent” is not used in isolation in RCW 82.08.986(3)(c), but is instead
used as part of a defined phrase: “new permanent employment position.” The term as used in the
definition refers to the quality of the positions to be filled—that is, they are not short-term and
impermanent positions as opposed to the permanent, “long-term jobs that provide living wages”
first contemplated by the Legislature in Laws of 2010, 1st sp. sess., ch. 1, § 1.
The statute does not require the employment to begin at a time certain after the certificate is issued
in order to be a “new permanent employment position” under RCW 82.08.986(3)(c). It only
requires that the position does not exist or not be filled before the exemption certificate is issued,
and that it meet certain hourly and wage minimums and other criteria within the six-year statutory
period.
Employee B
RCW 82.08.986 has no duration of employment requirement, and does not mandate that an
employee must work for the entirety of the six-year statutory period in order for the position to
qualify and be included in the calculation of net new permanent employee positions for purposes
of RCW 82.08.986(3)(a)(ii). The statute only requires the certificate holder to show that the
employee is filling a full-time position, and that the position meets the wage minimum threshold
and other statutory criteria at some point in the six-year period after the certificate was issued.
Although in part of 2015 and 2016, Employee B was on disability pay, his position was still
considered a full-time position on Taxpayer’s employee rolls, and it met the statutory criteria in
other years. Therefore, Employee B’s position should be included in the calculation of net new
permanent employ[ment] positions over the six-year period for purposes of RCW
82.08.986(3)(a)(ii). Because we resolve this issue on other grounds, we need not address the topic
of disability pay raised by Audit and Taxpayer.
Although we conclude that Employee B’s position meets the employment requirements for the
sales tax exemption in RCW 82.08.986, Employee A’s position does not, and thus Taxpayer has
not shown that it achieved a net of at least six new permanent employment positions during the
six-year audit period for purposes of RCW 82.08.986(3)(a)(ii). For the same reasons, Taxpayer
has not met the use tax exemption requirements in RCW 82.12.986. Because Taxpayer has not met
6 We note that in order to be a “qualifying tenant” to whom a certificate can be issued, the plain language of RCW
82.08.986(6)(i) states that the applicant must be “a business entity that exists for the primary purpose of engaging in
commercial activity for profit and that leases space from a qualifying business within an eligible computer data
center.” (Emphasis added.) Thus, either Taxpayer was not eligible for a data center exemption certificate, or it showed
when applying for the certificate that it had at least a substantive pending lease agreement of some kind with the owner
of the Data Center building. If the latter, Taxpayer likely had some possessory rights in the Data Center as of the date
the Exemption Certificate was issued, at the latest.

Det. No. 20-0129, 45 WTD 071 (June 9, 2026) 79
its burden of showing its entitlement to the data center exemptions in RCW 82.08.986 and RCW
82.12.986, we must deny the petition.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied.

description: An event-merchandise vending company (Taxpayer) protests an assessment by the Department of Revenue (Department). The Department’s assessment included adjustments for unpaid retail sales tax and service and other activities B&O tax. The Department also imposed an evasion penalty on Taxpayer for not remitting to the state the retail sales taxes it collected. Taxpayer contends that, as a consignee, it collected the retail sales tax on behalf of consignors, and it was not obligated to remit the retail sales tax to the state. However, some adjustments with respect to the assessment and in favor of Taxpayer, are warranted. We deny the petition in part and grant in part.

ANALYSIS
1. Seller and Seller’s Obligations
Washington imposes a retail sales tax on every retail sale of tangible personal property in the state.
RCW 82.08.020(1). “Sale” means any transfer of the ownership of, title to, or possession of
property for a valuable consideration. RCW 82.04.040(1). The term “retail sale” includes every
sale of tangible personal property, subject to certain exclusions, none of which apply here. RCW
82.04.050(1). Sellers must collect the full amount of the retail sales tax payable from buyers. RCW
82.08.050(1). If the seller fails to collect retail sales tax from the buyer or collects the tax and fails
to “pay it in the manner prescribed” to the Department, the seller becomes personally liable for the
amount of the tax whether the failure is the result of the seller’s actions or acts or conditions outside
of its control. RCW 82.08.050(3).
The term “seller” is a person “making sales at retail or retail sales to a buyer, purchaser, or
consumer, whether as agent, broker, or principal.” RCW 82.08.010(2). Here, Taxpayer asserts that
it is not responsible for remitting the retail sales tax because it is a consignee. Under Washington’s
tax code:
Every consignee, bailee, factor, or auctioneer having either actual or constructive
possession of personal property, or having possession of the documents of title thereto,
with power to sell such personal property in that person's own name and actually so
selling, is deemed the seller of such personal property within the meaning of this
chapter. Furthermore, the consignor, bailor, principal, or owner is deemed a seller of
such property to the consignee, bailee, factor, or auctioneer.
RCW 82.04.480(1) (emphasis added). When the consignee is deemed the seller, the consignee
“must collect and remit” the retail sales tax on each sale made. RCW 82.08.040(2)(a).
Taxpayer does not dispute that it had actual possession of the personal property with the power to
sell such personal property. Taxpayer argues that as a consignee it was not selling in its own name
but as an agent of the Consignors. However, under the Department’s administrative rule
implementing RCW 82.04.480, the “mere fact” that a consignee makes a sale “raises a
presumption” that the consignee sold in its name, and the “presumption is controlling unless
rebutted by proof satisfactory to the department of revenue.” Rule 159. Thus, “[t]he burden is on
the taxpayer in every case to establish the fact that the taxpayer is not engaged in the business of
making retail sales or wholesale sales but is acting merely as broker or agent in promoting sales
for a principal.” RCW 82.04.480(2); see Det. No. 08-0301, 28 WTD 68, 71 (2009) (“Sellers of
property are taxable on that activity unless they meet their statutory burden of proving that their
status was something other than that of seller.”). Accordingly, unless Taxpayer met the statutory
burden, Taxpayer was obligated to remit the taxes it collected to the state.
As a threshold matter, remittance to the state by consignors instead of the consignee is only allowed
when the consignor “is engaged in the business of selling tangible property” and the sale by the
consignee was made in the consignor’s name and the consignor “continues to be in business.” Rule
159. Taxpayer asserts that the Consignors, generally, are remitting the retail sales taxes. Taxpayer,

When a seller collects retail sales tax from customers, the amount “is deemed to be held in trust

if any seller, . . ., having collected the tax, fails to pay it to the department . . .,
whether the failure is the result of the seller’s own acts or the result or acts beyond
the seller’s control, the seller is, nevertheless, personally liable to the state for the
amount of the tax.
RCW 82.08.050(3). Sellers are specifically prohibited from appropriating or converting the tax

Inherent in RCW 82.08 is the fact that taxes collected in the name of the state are
not property of the seller. It is a misdemeanor to convert taxes collected to one’s
own use. The integrity of the entire taxing system demands that funds collected as
taxes be remitted to the state.

3. Evasion Penalty
The Department also imposed the evasion penalty against the unpaid retail sales tax and unpaid
service and other activities B&O tax. A fifty percent penalty “must be” imposed when the
Department finds that “all or any part of the deficiency resulted from an intent to evade” a tax due.
RCW 82.32.090(7). The Department’s rule explains when the application of the penalty is
warranted:
The evasion penalty is imposed when a taxpayer knows a tax liability is due but
attempts to escape detection or payment of the tax liability through deceit, fraud, or
other intentional wrongdoing. An intent to evade does not exist where a deficiency
is the result of an honest mistake, miscommunication, or the lack of knowledge
regarding proper accounting methods. The department has the burden of showing
the existence of an intent to evade a tax liability through clear, cogent and
convincing evidence.
Rule 228(5)(f). As such, there are two elements to establish with clear, cogent, and convincing
evidence of an “intent to evade”: (1) knowledge of a tax liability and (2) an attempt to escape
detection or payment through deceit, fraud, or other intentional wrongdoing. Id.; Det. No. 13-0329,
33 WTD 156, 158 (2013). Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence has been described as evidence
convincing the trier of fact that the issue is “highly probable,” or, stated another way, the evidence
must be “clear, positive, and unequivocal.” Colonial Imports, Inc. v. Carlton Northwest, Inc., 121
Wn.2d 726, 735, 853 P.2d 913 (1993) (citation omitted).
There is clear and convincing evidence of Taxpayer’s knowledge of the tax liability. Business or
tax experience “tends to undercut or negate the possibility that a taxpayer was unaware that it was
required to report and pay taxes.” Det. No. 04-0098, 23 WTD 331, 338 (2004) (internal citation
omitted). Here, Taxpayer had business and tax experience, specifically a prior audit, that indicated
it was aware or should have been aware it must report and remit the retail sales taxes collected.

willfully fails to remit to the Department the retail sales taxes collected from customers. Rule
228(5)(f)(ii)(B). It is undisputed that notwithstanding the prior audit, Taxpayer collected retail
sales tax and still did not remit to the state as obligated. Furthermore, Taxpayer’s excise tax filings

excise tax returns. Filing as an agent making consignment sales requires the following:
