In 33 WTD 156, we upheld an evasion penalty when the taxpayer put forth a similar argument. In
that administrative review, the taxpayer argued that the mistake was that it filed in a manner similar
to a predecessor-in-interest. However, it was undisputed that, like here, the taxpayer knowingly
charged retail sales tax, willfully retained the amounts collected, and consciously did not report
them as taxes due when filing its excise tax returns. Id. at 159. Although the reason for the honest
mistake is different than in this case, the facts are similar in that Taxpayer collected the retail sales
tax, willfully refrained from remitting, and consciously did not report them as taxes due in its
8 Although this Special Notice was issued during the Audit Period, and not prior to, it merely compiled the law and
rules and did not alter any taxpayer responsibilities. Additionally, Taxpayer had been made aware of its responsibility
for remitting the retail sales tax collected by a prior audit.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 103
excise tax returns. And in that case, we determined that the Department met its burden of proof
with regards to the evasion penalty.
Finally, Taxpayer asserts that Det. No. 92-133, 12 WTD 171 (1993) stands for a Department policy
that payment of a prior evasion penalty does not prove evasion in a latter case. In 12 WTD 171,
there were two factors mitigating in the taxpayers’ favor that led us to cancel the evasion penalty.
First, the taxpayers sought advice from a tax attorney in their attempt at legal tax avoidance of
motor vehicle excise tax (MVET). Id. at 9. Second, because the . . . [taxpayers’] used the motor
vehicle at issue only sparingly in Washington, there was clear and cogent evidence that the
taxpayers may have been uncertain the MVET was due. Id. For those reasons, a prior evasion
penalty imposed on the taxpayer’s failure to pay MVET on a different motor vehicle was not
sufficient to again impose the evasion penalty. Id. Here, the mitigating factors are not present.
There is no evidence that Taxpayer conferred with tax professionals on how to lawfully comply
with Washington’s tax laws. It is also indisputable that Taxpayer was aware of its obligation to
report and also remit the retail sales taxes collected. As such, we find that 12 WTD 171 does not
provide a rationale for canceling the evasion penalty in this case.
Having considered Taxpayer’s evidence, we do not find that Taxpayer has demonstrated an honest
mistake, miscommunication, ignorance of law, lack of knowledge, or some other fact that tends to
rebut the Department’s evidence. Furthermore, the Department has routinely upheld the evasion
penalty where sales tax was collected but not remitted. See Det. No. 13-0329, 33 WTD 156, 159
(2013); Det. No. 14-0268, 33 WTD 637, 641 (2014); Det. No. 04-0098, 23 WTD 331, 339 (2004)
(“Any attempt to evade payment of collected retail sales tax is a serious matter.”).
Audit Division also imposed the evasion penalty against assessed service and other activities B&O
tax. However, there is not clear and cogent evidence of evasion of the tax due on providing
security, and we have cancelled assessment of the tax against commissions and credit card fees.
Thus, we uphold the imposition of the evasion penalty only as assessed against the unremitted
retail sales taxes collected but not remitted. See Rule 228(5)(f)(i) (stating the evasion penalty
applies only to the specific taxes that the taxpayer intended to evade).
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer’s petition is denied in part and granted in part.
Dated this 17th day of March 2022.

gross income.

7

were charged 100% to the individual. Profit participation was determined annually. Taxpayer stated that the purported
joint venture maintained a master general ledger with sub-ledgers for each participant.

Det. No. 23-0042R, 45 WTD 109 (June 9, 2026) 114
ANALYSIS
The state of Washington imposes B&O tax on every person “for the act or privilege of engaging
in business activities” and the amount of tax is determined by the measure of the gross income of
the business. RCW 82.04.220. “Business” for B&O tax purposes includes “all activities engaged
in with the object of gain, benefit, or advantage to the taxpayer or to another person or class,
directly or indirectly.” RCW 82.04.140. Similarly, the term “gross income of the business” is
broadly defined as “the value proceeding or accruing by reason of the transaction of the business
engaged in and includes gross proceeds of sales, compensation for the rendition of services, . . .
and other emoluments however designated,” without any deduction for the costs or expenses of
the business. RCW 82.04.080(1).
The term “value proceeding or accruing” is defined as “the consideration, whether money, credits,
rights, or other property expressed in terms of money, actually received or accrued.” RCW
82.04.090. The receipt of money or credits as reimbursement for the costs of providing services is
value proceeding or accruing by reason of the transaction of business, even though no profit is
realized. Pullman Co. v. State, 65 Wn.2d 860, 867, 400 P.2d 91 (1965); Getty Images (Seattle) Inc.
v. City of Seattle, 163 Wn. App. 590, 606, 260 P.3d 926 (2011). Since the amount received is
“value proceeding or accruing” under RCW 82.04.090, it is “gross income of the business” under
RCW 82.04.080(1). In this case, the amount received is gross income of Taxpayer’s business.
These statutes all advance the Legislature’s intent “to impose the business and occupation tax upon
virtually all business activities carried on within the state.” Simpson Inv. Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue,
141 Wn.2d 139, 149, 3 P.3d 741 (2000) (quoting Time Oil Co. v. State, 79 Wn.2d 143, 483 P.2d
628 (1971)). “Broader language could hardly be devised to convey the idea implicit in [these]
definitions that the tax applies to everything that is earned, received, paid over to or acquired by
the seller.” Engine Rebuilders, Inc. v. State, 66 Wn.2d 147, 150, 401 P.2d 628 (1965).
Washington’s B&O tax is pyramiding in nature. See Det. No. 10-0197, 30 WTD 61 (2011); Det.
No. 88-370, 7 WTD 5 (1988); Det. No. 88-197, 5 WTD 369 (1988).
While the B&O tax applies broadly, tax exemption or deductions apply narrowly. The intent to
exempt gross income from taxation must be clear from the language of the statute. TracFone
Wireless, Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 170 Wn.2d 273, 296-97, 242 P.3d 810 (2010); see also Bravern
Residential, II, LLC v. Dep’t of Revenue, 183 Wn. App. 769, 778, 334 P.3d 1182 (2014) (“Tax
exemptions may not be created by implication.”). Consistent with these guiding principles, B&O
tax applies “unless a specific exemption exists.” Dot Foods, Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 185 Wn.2d
239, 245, 372 P.3d 747 (2016).
There is no general B&O tax exemption for amounts received by a business entity from a related
entity.9 Consequently, when a business entity sells goods or provides services to a related entity
for compensation, B&O tax applies. Wash. Sav-Mor Oil Co. v. Tax Commission, 58 Wn.2d 518,
523, 364 P.2d 440 (1961). In Washington Sav-Mor Oil, the taxpayer argued that wholesale sales it
made to its parent, Time Oil Company, should be disregarded for purposes of the state’s B&O tax
9 In 2013, the Legislature enacted a targeted B&O tax exemption for a business that provides qualified “paymaster
services” to its affiliates. See RCW 82.04.43393. Taxpayer does not assert that any of its gross income is exempt under
that statute.

Det. No. 23-0042R, 45 WTD 109 (June 9, 2026) 115
because taxpayer was “in reality only a part of Time Oil Company, and one cannot make a sale to
oneself.” Id. at 521. The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that a corporation is a
separate legal entity from its owners and that “courts will ignore the fiction of corporate entity
only with caution, and when the circumstances justify it, and when it is used as a subterfuge to . . .
perpetrate a fraud.” Id. at 523. The Court further explained that “[t]he legislature has not seen fit
to exclude transactions between affiliated corporations, and we find in the facts of this case nothing
which would justify the judicial engrafting of such an exclusion upon the statute.” Id. . . . .
The Court of Appeals applied the same principle in Getty Images, holding that amounts the
taxpayer received as reimbursement for administrative and managerial services provided to its
subsidiaries was gross income of the business and subject to the City of Seattle’s local B&O tax.[10]
Getty Images, 163 Wn. App. 590 at 606. The party providing those services, Getty Images (Seattle)
Inc., was a separate entity from its affiliates and the “broad definition of gross income and
‘emoluments however designated’ includes the receipt of . . . funds by Getty Seattle to pay for the
services provided” to its affiliates. Id. at 606-07.
There is no legal or logical reason why the B&O tax principle applied in Washington Sav-Mor Oil
and Getty Images would apply differently with respect to a joint venture. See, Impecoven v. Dep’t
of Revenue, 120 Wn.2d 357, 361, 841 P.2d 752 (1992) (rejecting the contention that B&O tax did
not apply to insurance commissions received from affiliated insurance agents merely because the
parties to the transaction were a “group of individuals acting as a unit”); Cf. Bravern Residential,
II, [183 Wn. App. at 779] (under Washington law, there is no recognized exception that permits a
contractor to avoid sales tax and B&O tax on construction services performed on land of a “co-
venturer”). It is well established that a business entity, including a joint venture, is a separate
“person” from its owners. Dep’t of Revenue v. Nord Nw. Corp., 164 Wn. App. 215, 230, 264 P.3d
259, 266 (2011).
If a joint venture between Taxpayer and the Related Entities did exist, the unnamed joint venture
would be a separate “person” under the B&O tax code. See RCW 82.04.030 and RCW 82.04.220.
The joint venture engaging in business under RCW 82.04.066 would be subject to B&O tax under
RCW 82.04.270.11 Therefore, the existence of a joint venture agreement between the parties is
irrelevant as it does not alter the taxability of amounts received by Taxpayer in exchange for its
provision of services to the purported joint venturers. Consequently, amounts Taxpayer received
for services it provided to the venture or to other co-venturers would be subject to B&O tax unless
an express exemption exists.
Even if we were to assume a joint venture existed, Taxpayer has not established how the income
at issue would not be subject to B&O tax. In general, “[t]axation is the rule and exemption is the
exception.” Budget Rent–A–Car, 81 Wn.2d 171, 174, 500 P.2d 764 (1972). Exemptions and
deductions are “tax preferences” under RCW 43.136.021, and must be “[construed] strictly . . .
though fairly and in keeping with the ordinary meaning of their language, against the taxpayer.”
[Group Health Coop. of Puget Sound, Inc. v. Washington State Tax Comm'n, 72 Wn.2d 422, 429,
[10 The principles applied by Court of Appeals in Getty Images to the City of Seattle's B&O tax are relevant here as
the City of Seattle's definition of gross income for B&O purposes is substantively identical to the definition of gross
income used in RCW 82.04.080(1) (See SMC 5.30.035(D) (incorporated by SMC 5.45.030)).]
11 The purported joint venture did not register with the Department or file and pay excise tax liability during the tax
period.

Det. No. 23-0042R, 45 WTD 109 (June 9, 2026) 116
433 P.2d 201 (1967))] Further, “[w]hen interpreting . . . deduction provisions, ‘the burden of
showing qualification for the tax benefit . . . rests with the taxpayer . . . .’” Simpson Investment Co.
v. Dep’t of Revenue, 141 Wn.2d 139, 149-50, 3 P.3d 741 (2000), (quoting Group Health, [72
Wn.2d at 429 ]. See Stroh Brewing Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 104 Wash. App. 235, 240, 15 P.3d
692 (2001) (“[t]he taxpayer has the burden of establishing eligibility for an exemption”); see also
Port of Seattle v. State, 101 Wn. App. 106, 1 P.3d 607 (2000) (“exemption statutes are construed
strictly against the taxpayer, and the taxpayer has the burden of establishing any exemption”).
Every taxpayer is therefore responsible for being able to demonstrate that it qualifies for each
claimed deduction under a strictly construed interpretation of the rules.
Taxpayer has not explained what exemption would cover reimbursements for costs in a joint
venture situation. While the Department has held that distributions of profits to a member of a joint
venture are nontaxable, payments for services rendered are not. See Det. No. 99-176. 19 WTD 456
(2000), citing to Det. No. 90-74, 3 WTD 431 (1990). Furthermore, based on the definition of
“person” in RCW 82.04.030 and other related B&O tax statutes, Washington Courts have
respected the different persons engaging in business in Washington State, even though those
persons may be affiliated with each other in some manner. See, e.g., Impecoven, 120 Wn.2d 357
(independent contractor insurance agents affiliated with broker are not one “person” for B&O tax
purposes and not “group of individuals acting as a unit” under RCW 82.04.030.); Nordstrom
Credit, Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 120 Wn.2d 935, 845 P.2d 1331 (1993) (subsidiary formed by
parent to finance parent’s accounts receivable engaged in arms-length transaction with parent and
was a separate “person” for B&O tax purposes); American Sign & Indicator Corp. v. State, 93
Wn.2d 427, 429, 610 P.2d 353 (1980) (“The tax liability of a corporation must be considered
without regard to its relationship to a parent or subsidiary company or to the existence of common
officers, employees, facilities, or stock ownership.”). Washington law treats different entities as
different persons, each subject to B&O tax on their taxable activities. See RCW 82.04.220. There
is no basis for concluding that payments between entities that form a joint venture together or
payments from a joint venture to one of the members for services rendered to the joint venture are
not subject to B&O tax. See also Bravern Residential II, LLC, [183 Wn. App. 769].
The result treats Taxpayer the same whether it is related to the entities for which it provides
services, or not. If the Related Entities receive the same services from an unrelated entity as those
provided by Taxpayer, and if those Related Entities pay the unrelated entity the exact amount it
paid to Taxpayer, that unrelated entity would owe B&O tax on its service income. There is no legal
or logical reason why the result should be different merely because the Related Entities entered
into service agreements with closely related entities instead of with an unrelated third party.
As our Supreme Court pointed out many years ago, “[s]tatutes providing for the raising of revenue
required by the state in carrying on its functions are vital to its welfare,” and any person, whether
natural or artificial, “should not be declared exempt from the payment of a tax required of business
generally, unless it clearly appears that the constitution and laws of the United States (or of the
state) require such exemption.” North Pac. Coast Freight Bureau v. State, 12 Wn.2d 563, [571],
122 P.2d 467 (1942) (quoting Fisher’s Blend Station v. State Tax Comm’n, 182 Wash. 163, 167, 45
P.2d 942 (1935)). There is no “joint venture” exemption or exclusion to the B&O tax, and Taxpayer
is not immune from the tax even if it had formed a joint venture with the Related Entities. Having
determined that the existence of a joint venture between Taxpayer and the Related Entities is not
determinative of Taxpayer’s B&O tax liability, we do not consider further whether Taxpayer has

Det. No. 23-0042R, 45 WTD 109 (June 9, 2026) 117
established the existence of such a joint venture. As discussed above, amounts received by
Taxpayer from the Related Entities for Taxpayer’s providing services to the Related Entities is
gross income to Taxpayer. We deny Taxpayer’s petition.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied.
Dated this 2nd day of October 2023.

ANALYSIS
RCW 82.32A.030 provides that taxpayers have the responsibility to pay taxes in a timely manner.
If the Department obtains information from which it appears a person has not paid the amount of
tax properly due, then the Department is required to assess any additional amounts found due
against that person and is also required to add interest to the tax due. RCW 82.32.050.
RCW 82.32.090(2) states that there is assessed a penalty of 5-percent when the Department
determines that a taxpayer has substantially underpaid a tax that was due. If payment is not
received by the due date specified in the notice, there is assessed a total penalty of 15-percent and,
if payment is not received on or before the thirtieth day following the due date specified in the
notice, there is assessed a total penalty of 25-percent. “Substantially underpaid” means the
taxpayer has paid less than 80 percent of the tax due and the underpayment is at least $1,000.00. Id.
1. Waiver on Grounds of Cyberattack
The Department has limited authority to waive or cancel penalties under RCW 82.32.105.
Generally, the Department will not waive penalties unless the failure that triggered the penalty was
the result of “circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer.” RCW 82.32.105(1).
WAC 458-20-228 (Rule 228) explains that “[c]ircumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer
are generally those which are immediate, unexpected, or in the nature of an emergency. Such
circumstances result in the taxpayer not having reasonable time or opportunity to obtain an
extension of the due date or otherwise timely file and pay.” Rule 228(9)(a)(ii). The burden is on
the taxpayer to establish that “the circumstances were beyond its control and directly caused the
late payment.” Rule 228(9)(a)(i).

In this matter, Taxpayer argues that a cyberattack suffered by Payment Processor resulted in
Taxpayer not having sufficient cash to timely pay its tax liability. Examples of what generally
constitutes circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer are provided in Rule 228(9)(a)(ii),
none of which apply to the situation under consideration.4 Rule 228(9)(a)(iii) also gives examples
of circumstances that are generally not considered to be a basis for waiving penalties.5 This
includes financial hardship.
In Det. No. 87-189, 3 WTD 223 (1987), the taxpayer was in the healthcare business, received
approximately 40 percent of its income from the state of Washington, and the state’s payments
were frequently months delinquent. We concluded that the state’s late payment of amounts due to
the taxpayer could not justify a penalty waiver, explaining as follows:
It makes no difference that the state is the contracting party with the taxpayer. Our
holding would be the same even if the contracting party were a private business. In
other words, a person’s tax liability is an absolute; it is no defense that other third
4 Examples of circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer in Rule 228(9)(a)(ii) include:
(A) The return payment was mailed on time but inadvertently sent to another agency.
(B) Erroneous written information given to the taxpayer by a department officer or employee caused the delinquency
. . . .
(C) The delinquency was directly caused by death or serious illness of the taxpayer, or a member of the taxpayer’s
immediate family . . . .
(D) The delinquency was caused by the unavoidable absence of the taxpayer or key employee, prior to the filing date.
“Unavoidable absence of the taxpayer” does not include absences because of business trips, vacations, personnel

(E) The delinquency was caused by the destruction by fire or other casualty of the taxpayer’s place of business or

(F) The delinquency was caused by an act of fraud, embezzlement, theft, or conversion on the part of the taxpayer’s
employee or other persons contracted with the taxpayer, which the taxpayer could not immediately detect or prevent,
provided that reasonable safeguards or internal controls were in place. See (a)(iii)(E) of this subsection.
(G) The department does not respond to the taxpayer’s request for a tax return (or other forms necessary to compute
the tax) within a reasonable period of time, which directly causes delinquent filing and payment on the part of the

pending due dates) and must anticipatively request a return for that purpose, if one is not received . . . .

(A) Financial hardship;

Here, Taxpayer alleges that cash flow problems prevented timely payment. However, financial
hardship is not grounds for waiver, regardless of whether Payment Processor suffered a
cyberattack and failed to timely process claims. Thus, we find that the cyberattack was not a
circumstance beyond Taxpayer’s control that qualifies Taxpayer for waiver. See also, Det. No. 06-
0267, 26 WTD 159 (2007). Further, we note that Taxpayer’s waiver request submitted with its
return explains that the late filing was also due to an error on account of a newborn, but mistakes
are generally not considered beyond the control of the taxpayer per Rule 228(9)(a)(iii)(E). Because
Taxpayer failed to prove that “circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer” directly caused
the late payment, we conclude that Taxpayer does not qualify for waiver of the assessment penalty.
RCW 82.32.105(3) and Rule 228(10) provide that the Department will waive or
cancel interest imposed under chapter 82.32 RCW only where the failure to pay the tax prior to
the issuance of the assessment was the direct result of written instructions given the taxpayer by
the Department, or the extension of the due date for payment of an assessment was not at the
request of the taxpayer and was for the sole convenience of the Department. Since we find no
evidence of either of these circumstances in the petition or record, these provisions provide no
grounds for abatement of interest.
2. Waiver on Grounds of Oral Advice
Taxpayer argues that it was given oral advice to wait for contact regarding a payment plan, which
resulted in the accrual of additional liability. Rule 228(9)(a)(ii)(B) provides, in pertinent part, that
[a] penalty generally will not be waived when it is claimed that erroneous oral
information was given by a department employee. The reason for not canceling the
penalty in cases of oral information is because of the uncertainty of the facts
presented, the uncertainty of the instructions or information imparted by the
department employee, and the uncertainty that the taxpayer fully understood the
information given. . . [.]
Excise Tax Advisory (ETA) 3065.20096 discusses oral instructions related to tax liability as
follows:
RCW 82.32A.020 provides that the taxpayers of Washington have:: [sic]
The right to rely on specific, official written advice and written tax
reporting instructions from the department of revenue to that
taxpayer, and to have interest, penalties, and in some instances, tax
deficiency assessments waived where the taxpayer has so relied to
their proven detriment.
6 ETAs are interpretive statements authorized by RCW 34.05.230.
Administrative Review & Hearings Division
P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 25-0060, 45 WTD 124 (June 9, 2026) 129
RCW 82.32A.020 does not authorize, nor does any other law permit, the
Department to waive tax, interest, or penalties on the basis of a taxpayer’s
recollection of oral instructions by an agent of the department.
The Department gives consideration, to the extent of discretion vested in it by law,
where it can be shown that failure of a taxpayer to report correctly was due to
written instructions from the Department or any of its authorized agents. The
Department cannot give consideration to claimed misinformation resulting from
telephone conversations or personal consultations with a Department employee.
There are three reasons for this ruling:
(1) There is no record of the facts which might have been presented
to the employee for consideration.
(2) There is no record of instructions or information imparted by the
employee, which may have been erroneous or incomplete.
(3) There is no evidence that such instructions were completely
understood or followed by the taxpayer.
(Underlining in original.)
Because we find no written evidence that Taxpayer was advised to pay nothing and wait for contact
regarding a payment plan, and the law does not permit the Department to waive penalties or interest
based on Taxpayer’s recollection of oral instructions, we find no grounds for relief.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer’s petition is denied.

RCW 82.08.9998: EXEMPTIONS – RECORD KEEPING REQUIREMENTS
FOR CANNABIS PRODUCTS EXEMPTION. The legislature explicitly granted
the Department the authority to determine the “information establishing eligibility
for the exemption” a taxpayer must maintain to qualify for this exemption. The
Department established those criteria for in a special notice issued May 6, 2016.

Kelly, T.R.O. – Two marijuana1 retailers protest the Department’s assessments to the extent the
Department disallowed [exemptions] for sales of marijuana to customers made prior to the
issuance of the customers’ patient recognition card ID numbers. Taxpayers contend that their
point-of-sale software did not maintain a copy of the original ID number when customers got new
recognition cards with new ID numbers. While marijuana products can be exempt from taxation
under RCW 82.08.9998, Taxpayers did not follow the recordkeeping requirements. We deny the
petition.2
ISSUES
Have Taxpayers provided the Department with suitable records under WAC 458-20-254 (Rule
254) to prove certain sales of marijuana products are exempt from retail sales tax under RCW
82.08.9998?
FINDINGS OF FACT
[Taxpayer] doing business as [Entity 1] and [Entity 2] (referred to as Taxpayers) are affiliated
entities operating as recreational and medical marijuana retailers selling marijuana products and
paraphernalia . . . .
1 The term “marijuana” was the statutory term for the entirety of the audit period. Through SSHB 1210, Chapter 16,
Laws of 2022 (effective June 9, 2022), the [l]egislature replaced the term “marijuana” with the term “cannabis.”
2
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 23-0051, 45 WTD 044 (May 5, 2026) 45
The Department of Revenue’s (Department’s) Audit Division (Audit) inspected both Taxpayers’
records for the period of January 1, 2018, through June 30, 2021 (Audit Period).
Taxpayers possess medical cannabis endorsements. This allows Taxpayers to make sales tax
exempt sales of qualifying products to customers with qualifying patient recognition cards.
Audit reviewed Taxpayers’ records to verify the sales to customers with qualifying patient
recognition cards.
Taxpayers did not retain copies of customers’ patient recognition cards. Instead, Taxpayers’
[point-of-sale system] retained reports containing records of individual transactions and associated
patient recognition card ID numbers.
Audit compared the provided ID Numbers to the Department of Health’s database. This process
revealed several issues including (1) sales of non-qualifying marijuana paraphernalia products, (2)
sales to ID Numbers that were expired at the time of sale, (3) and sales to ID Numbers prior to
their date of issuance. Audit came to understand that instead of creating a new profile for a
customer when that customer received a new ID Number, Taxpayers overrode that customer’s
prior number with the new one. This resulted in the point-of-sale system not retaining the prior ID
Number. As Taxpayers retained no documentation, these sales were disallowed.
On May 27, 2022, Audit issued [Letter 1] to [Entity 1] for a total of $. . . .3
On May 27, 2022, Audit issued [Letter 2] to [Entity 2] for a total of $. . . .4
Taxpayers timely filed petitions for administrative review. Subsequently, Taxpayers clarified that
they were not contesting the adjustments to the extent that they related to sales of non-qualifying
marijuana paraphernalia products or sales to ID Numbers that were expired at the time of sale.
Taxpayers are only contesting the adjustments to the extent they relate to sales made prior to
medical card issuance. Taxpayers contend that the original ID Number data had been overridden
but valid records existed at the time of sale.
Taxpayers made repeated attempts to get more detailed information from [point-of-sale system]
with limited results. Eventually Taxpayers provided additional records to bolster their argument,
including a spreadsheet prepared by [point-of-sale system] showing ID Numbers, point-of-sale
device identification, receipt numbers, dates of sale, employee names, patient names when
available, and other transaction detail.
Audit reviewed the information but did not believe it warranted adjustment to the assessments. As

issuance.

ANALYSIS
Washington requires persons making retail sales to collect and remit retail sales tax unless an
exemption applies. RCW 82.08.020; RCW 82.08.050. “Retail sale” is statutorily defined and
includes the sale of tangible personal property. RCW 82.04.050(1)(a). “Tangible personal
property” means property that can be “seen, weighed, measured, felt, or touched . . . .” WAC 458-
20-193(1)(c). Generally, the sale of marijuana is a retail sale subject to retail sales tax as tangible
property. Accordingly, Taxpayer must remit retail sales tax for retail sales and pay retailing
business and occupation (B&O) tax on its gross proceeds of sales unless an exemption applies.
RCW 82.08.020; RCW 82.04.250.
The legislature provides an exemption from retail sales tax for the sale of certain marijuana
products by marijuana retailers with marijuana endorsements to qualifying patients or designated
providers who have been issued recognition cards. RCW 82.08.9998(1)(a). Taxpayers are
marijuana retailers with a medical marijuana endorsement. Because RCW 82.08.9998 provides an
exemption from a prescribed tax, we construe its application narrowly. See Budget Rent-A-Car,
Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 81, Wn.2d 171, 500 P.2d 764 (1972); Det. No 01-007, 20 WTD 214, 231
(2001) (stating the Department construes exemptions narrowly in favor of taxation). Additionally,
the taxpayer has the burden to prove the right to any exemption from taxation. See Det. No. 19-
0185R, 40 WTD 231, 234 (2021).
RCW 82.08.9998 includes the requirements to claim the exemption. Namely, “Each seller making
exempt sales under subsection (1) of this section must maintain information establishing eligibility
for the exemption in the form and manner required by the department.” RCW 82.08.9998. In RCW
82.08.9998, the “department” refers to the Department of Revenue. See RCW 82.02.010(2). In
RCW 82.08.9998(2), the legislature explicitly granted the Department the authority to determine
the “information establishing eligibility for the exemption” a taxpayer must maintain.
Every taxpayer “must” keep and preserve, for a period of five years, “suitable records” as may be
necessary to determine the tax for which taxpayer is liable. RCW 82.32.070(1). WAC 458-20-254
is the Department’s administrative rule detailing recordkeeping [and] explains further what
suitable records must be kept. With regards to exemptions, the taxpayer must keep “complete and
adequate records” to demonstrate the amounts of all exemptions claimed “through supporting
records or documentation required by statute or administrative rule, or other supporting records or
documentation necessary to substantiate” the deduction. Rule 254(3)(a)(ii). RCW 82.08.9998(2)
does not contain specific requirements but states the seller “must maintain information establishing
eligibility for the exemption in the form and manner required by the department.”
The Department clarified what information taxpayers must maintain for the retail sales and use tax
exemption for marijuana retailers with a medical endorsement by issuing a Special Notice on May
6, 2016 (Special Notice). In addition to the fact that the Special Notice predates the Audit Period,
it explicitly states it is intended for marijuana retailers with a medical endorsement, like Taxpayers.
Special Notice, p. 1. [The Department stated, u]nder the section titled “How do I document these
exemptions?” . . . :

Det. No. 23-0051, 45 WTD 044 (May 5, 2026) 47
Retailers must:
• Verify the qualifying patient or designated provider has a current recognition
card.
• Enter the qualifying patient or designated provider’s recognition card number
into LCB’s traceability system.
• Keep a copy of the qualifying patient or designated provider’s recognition card
as required by RCW 69.50.375[(3)](e). Retailers only need to keep one copy of
each valid recognition card and do not need to get multiple copies of the same
card for repeat customers.
• Keep records of tax exempt sales, including the applicable recognition card
number used by the purchaser, for at least five years.
Id. at 3. Taxpayers must satisfy every requirement in the notice.
In the instant case, Taxpayers fail two separate requirements, each of which individually would be
sufficient to deny the petition.
First, Taxpayers failed to keep a copy of the qualifying patient or designated provider’s recognition
cards. Taxpayers were required to keep copies of these cards and not merely equivalent
information under the Special Notice. While Taxpayers provided records to include ID Numbers,
point-of-sale device identification, receipt numbers, dates of sale, employee names, patient names
when available, and other transaction detail, Taxpayers did not provide copies of actual cards.
Second, Taxpayers failed the last requirement. In overriding ID Numbers in their . . . point-of-sale
system, Taxpayers lost any records of applicable ID Numbers they had accepted for the sales.
While Taxpayers worked with [point-of-sale system] to prepare a spreadsheet, Taxpayers were
unable to retrieve any of this specific data. Taxpayers were required to keep this data for five years.
Taxpayers failed to do so, and Taxpayers’ records instead only contain records of sales to ID
Numbers prior to their date of issuance. Such records do not satisfy the recordkeeping requirement.
Taxpayers hold the burden to prove the right to any exemption. It is not the Department’s burden
or responsibility to verify tax exempt sales beyond Taxpayers’ records. Because Taxpayers cannot
verify tax exempt sales, Audit properly denied the exemption.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
We deny Taxpayers’ petition.
Dated this 13th day of March 2023.

much lesser extent.
The Department of Revenue’s (Department) Audit Division (Audit) reviewed Taxpayer’s books
and records for the tax period May 1, 2016, through October 31, 2020. On May 20, 2022, the

product development expenditures tax credit in the amount of $. . . . The Department’s denial of

You are not eligible for the requested aerospace product development credit due to
lack of substantiating documentation.
Taxpayer timely requested review. Taxpayer contends that the amount of gross income from
aerospace activities should be used as a proxy for the amount of expenses incurred in aerospace
product development. Taxpayer contends that the amount of gross income from its aerospace
activities can be verified using its excise tax returns.
2 . . .
3 The federal R&D study was commissioned by Taxpayer from its accounting firm . . . . A procedural manual provided

ANALYSIS
Washington imposes a B&O tax “for the act or privilege of engaging in business” in Washington.
RCW 82.04.220. The B&O tax measure and rate are determined by the type or nature of the
business activity in which a person is engaged. Chapter 82.04 RCW. The specific tax rate is
determined by the nature of the business activity in which a taxpayer is engaged. See generally
chapter 82.04 RCW.
The Legislature “intended to impose the business and occupation tax upon virtually all business
activities carried on within the state.” Simpson Inv. Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 141 Wn.2d 139, 149,
3 P.3d 741 (2000) (quoting Time Oil Co. v. State, 79 Wn.2d 143, 146, 483 P.2d 628 (1971)). The
B&O tax is not a tax on profit, net gain, capital gain, or sales “but a tax on the total money or
money’s worth received in the course of doing business.” Budget Rent-A-Car of Wash.-Oregon,
Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 81 Wn.2d 171, 172, 500 P.2d 764 (1972). The B&O tax provisions “leave
practically no business and commerce free of the business and occupation tax.” Id. at 175.
. . .
RCW 82.04.4461 provides a B&O tax credit for qualified preproduction development expenditures
for aerospace product development activities, as follows:
(1)(a)(i) In computing the tax imposed under this chapter, a credit is allowed
for each person for qualified aerospace product development. For a person who
is a manufacturer or processor for hire of commercial airplanes or components
of such airplanes, credit may be earned for expenditures occurring after
December 1, 2003. For all other persons, credit may be earned only for
expenditures occurring after June 30, 2008.
(2) The credit is equal to the amount of qualified aerospace product
development expenditures of a person, multiplied by the rate of 1.5 percent.
(4) Any person claiming the credit must file a form prescribed by the
department that must include the amount of the credit claimed, an estimate of
the anticipated aerospace product development expenditures during the
calendar year for which the credit is claimed, an estimate of the taxable amount
during the calendar year for which the credit is claimed, and such additional
information as the department may prescribe.
RCW 82.04.4461(5)(b) defines “aerospace product development” as:
[R]esearch, design, and engineering activities performed in relation to the
development of an aerospace product or of a product line, model, or model
derivative of an aerospace product, including prototype development, testing,
and certification.

Det. No. 23-0102, 45 WTD 054 (May 5, 2026) 57
RCW 82.32.070 requires taxpayers to maintain records adequate for the Department to determine
their tax liability. RCW 82.32.070(1) states, in relevant part:
Every taxpayer liable for any tax collected by the department must keep and
preserve, for a period of five years, suitable records as may be necessary to
determine the amount of any tax for which the taxpayer may be liable. Such records
must include copies of all of the taxpayer's federal income tax and state tax returns
and reports. All of the taxpayer's books, records, and invoices must be open for
examination at any time by the department of revenue. . . .
Rule 254 is the Department’s administrative rule regarding recordkeeping. Rule 254(3) states, in
relevant part:
(b) It is the duty of each taxpayer to prepare and preserve all records in a systematic
manner conforming to accepted accounting methods and procedures. Such records
are to be kept, preserved, and presented upon request of the department or its
authorized representatives which will demonstrate:
(i) The amounts of gross receipts and sales from all sources,
however derived, including barter or exchange transactions, whether
or not such receipts or sales are taxable. These amounts must be
supported by original source documents or records including but not
limited to all purchase invoices, sales invoices, contracts, and such
other records as may be necessary to substantiate gross receipts and
sales.
. . .
(c) The records kept, preserved, and presented must include the normal records
maintained by an ordinary prudent business person. Such records may include
general ledgers, sales journals, cash receipts journals, bank statements, check
registers, and purchase journals, together with all bills, invoices, cash register tapes,
and other records or documents of original entry supporting the books of account
entries. The records must include all federal and state tax returns and reports and
all schedules, work papers, instructions, and other data used in the preparation of
the tax reports or returns.
Taxpayer contends it is entitled to the credit available for qualified aerospace preproduction
development expenditures under RCW 82.04.4461(2). The credit is equal to the amount of
qualified aerospace product development expenditures multiplied by a rate of 1.5 percent. Id.
Under RCW 82.32.070(1), Taxpayer bears the burden of maintaining documentation necessary for
the Department to verify its tax liability. Under Rule 254, Taxpayer’s documentation must include
source documentation including purchase invoices . . . .
In this case, Taxpayer did not maintain source documentation in the ordinary course of business
tying expenditures to actual business activities or segregating expenditures by project. Taxpayer
concedes that some of its projects are not qualified aerospace development so we cannot conclude
that any specific expenditure falls within the definition of “aerospace product development” in

Det. No. 23-0102, 45 WTD 054 (May 5, 2026) 58
RCW 82.04.4461(5)(b). Under RCW 82.32.070(1) and Rule 254, Taxpayer fails to meet its burden
to provide documentation allowing the Department to verify its purported tax liability, including
its claim for the aerospace development credit under RCW 82.04.4461(1)(a)(i). Moreover, using
a subsequent estimate of R&D expenditures, calculated under IRC Sections 41 and 174, not the
definition of “qualified aerospace product development expenditures” under RCW 82.04.
4461(5)(d), would impermissibly expand the application of the [credit]. Likewise, employing a
proxy method for estimating qualified aerospace product development expenditures, like the gross
income from aerospace development proposed by Taxpayer, instead of requiring a taxpayer to
meet its burden under RCW 82.32.070(1) and Rule 254, would impermissibly expand the pool of
taxpayers eligible for the credit. . . .
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied.
Dated this 9th day of May 2023.

Taxpayer also argues that because it was placed on active nonreporting status during the periods
at issue, that it neither is required to file a tax return nor participate in audits. Finally, Taxpayer

such, he argues that the audit is based on presumptions and not facts. Taxpayer stated that while

[Address 3] property, he stated that he didn’t remember what that permit was for. He denied doing
any work on the [Address 4] property. The [Address 1] property is where he currently lives. He
argues that the [Address 5] property was built for him and his wife to live in but was forced to sell
it due to medical reasons.
ANALYSIS
1. Authority to Audit
The Washington tax system is based largely on voluntary compliance. The Revenue Act imposes
on taxpayers the responsibility to inform themselves about applicable tax laws, register with the
Department, and accurately and timely pay taxes. Ch. 82.32A RCW.
If the Department obtains information from which it appears a person has not paid the amount of
tax properly due, RCW 82.32.050(1) authorizes the Department to assess against a taxpayer “such

Det. No. 24-0003, 45 WTD 062 (May 5, 2026) 66
additional amount found to be due and shall add thereto interest” where “an examination of any
returns or from other information obtained by the department shows that a tax or penalty had been
paid less than properly due…” The Department may generally assess up to four years after the
close of the tax year but may assess for up to seven years under certain circumstances.3 RCW
82.32.050(4), WAC 458-20-230.
Here, while in the course of auditing an affiliated business, the Department noticed that business
had transferred $ . . . into Taxpayer’s bank account. When questioned about the transfer, Taxpayer
told Audit that the money was repaying a loan that it had issued the affiliated business. When asked
for supporting documentation, Taxpayer provided Audit only with a single page of a bank
statement, which outlined that it paid over $ . . . in checks in one month. This additional information
gave the Department reason to believe that Taxpayer had taxable income and had not paid the
amount of tax properly due. Thus, on August 2, 2022, the Department notified Taxpayer that it
intended to review its business activities from 2018 through 2022. Because the audit was completed
within four years after the close of the tax year 2018, the Department acted within its statutory
authority. RCW 82.32.050.
Taxpayer argues that the Department does not have the authority to audit a taxpayer that is an
affiliate of a business that is also subject to an audit. Taxpayer argues that because there is no rule
or statute that specifically authorizes the Department to audit affiliated businesses, it cannot do so.
We disagree. RCW 82.32.070 grants the Department the broad authority to audit “Every taxpayer,”
regardless of whether they are an affiliate of another business. Taxpayer then argues that it is not
subject to this broad authority because it was placed on “active nonreporting” status.
RCW 82.32.045(5) and WAC 458-20-101(3) (Rule 101) allow the Department to relieve
qualifying taxpayers from the requirement to file tax returns. Businesses assigned to this status are
not required to file excise tax returns. Businesses retain their Unified Business Identifier (UBI
number), and Department’s tax registration number, and are considered to be actively doing
business in Washington. To qualify for the “active nonreporting” status, all of the following criteria
must be met:
(i) The person's value of products (RCW 82.04.050), gross proceeds of sales (RCW
82.04.070), or gross income of the business (RCW 82.04.080), from all business
activities taxable under chapter 82.04 RCW (B&O tax), is less than $125,000;
(ii) The person's gross income (RCW 82.16.010) from all business activities taxable
under chapter 82.16 RCW (public utility tax) is less than $24,000 per year; and
(iii) The person is not required to collect or pay to the department retail sales tax or
any other tax or fee the department is authorized to collect.
WAC 458-20-101(3)(a). Being placed on active nonreporting status is not a permanent
designation, however. RCW 82.32A.030(2) requires taxpayers to “know their tax reporting
obligations, and when they are uncertain about their obligation, seek instructions from the
3 RCW 82.32.050(4) states that no assessment may be made by the department more than four years after the close of
the tax year, “except (a) against a taxpayer who has not registered as required by this chapter, (b) upon a showing of
fraud or of misrepresentation of a material fact by the taxpayer, or (c) where a taxpayer has executed a written waiver
of such limitation.”

Det. No. 24-0003, 45 WTD 062 (May 5, 2026) 67
department.” This includes the responsibility to know if they still qualify for active nonreporting
status. If a Taxpayer no longer meets any of Rule 101’s criteria, it is their responsibility to notify
the Department:
Persons placed on an active nonreporting status by the department are required to
timely notify the department if their business activities do not meet any of the
conditions explained in (a) of this subsection. These persons will be removed from
an active nonreporting status, and must file tax returns and remit appropriate taxes
to the department, beginning with the first period in which they do not qualify for
an active nonreporting status.
WAC 458-20-101(3)(c) (emphasis added).
Here, Taxpayer was placed on active nonreporting status prior to the Audit Period. Because
Taxpayer was not filing tax returns with the Department, it was Taxpayer’s sole responsibility to
notify the Department if it no longer qualified for that status. When Audit discovered Taxpayer
had both deposited $ . . . into its bank account and written over $ . . . in checks over the course of
two months, it had reason to believe that Taxpayer may be required to pay taxes to the Department.
Thus, Audit initiated an examination of Taxpayer’s business activities. As discussed above, RCW
82.32.070 authorizes the examination of any taxpayer’s records, even those in active nonreporting
status.
2. Assessed Amounts
As discussed above, RCW 82.32A.030 details taxpayer rights and responsibilities and charges
Taxpayers with the responsibility for keeping accurate and complete business records, filing
accurate returns and paying taxes in a timely manner. RCW 82.32A.030(3)(4).
RCW 82.32.070 expressly mandates taxpayers to provide adequate records to establish
their correct tax liability. It reads, in part:
Every taxpayer liable for any tax collected by the department must keep and
preserve, for a period of five years, suitable records as may be necessary to
determine the amount of any tax for which the taxpayer may be liable. Such records
must include copies of all of the taxpayer's federal income tax and state tax returns
and reports. All of the taxpayer's books, records, and invoices must be open for
examination at any time by the department of revenue. . . .
RCW 82.32.070(1).
Should a taxpayer fail to provide suitable records, RCW 82.32.100 provides the Department with
authority to estimate tax liability. RCW 82.32.100 reads, in pertinent part:
(1) If any person fails or refuses to make any return or to make available for
examination the records required by this chapter, the department shall proceed, in
such manner as it may deem best, to obtain facts and information on which to base

Det. No. 24-0003, 45 WTD 062 (May 5, 2026) 68
its estimate of the tax; and to this end the department may examine the records of
any such person as provided in RCW 82.32.110.
(Emphasis added.)
RCW 82.32.100 affords the Department wide discretion in the methodology employed to calculate
a reasonable estimate of tax. See Det. No. 15-0350, 35 WTD 291 (2015) (affirming the
Department’s authority to assess taxes based on a reasonable estimate and citing Det. No. 14-0106,
33 WTD 402 (2014); Det. No. 13-0302R, 33 WTD 572 (2014); Det. No. 03-0279, 23 WTD (2004);
and Det. No. 97-134R, 18 WTD 163 (1999)). An abuse of discretion occurs when a decision rests
on untenable grounds or is manifestly unreasonable. Mayer v. Sto Indus., Inc., 156 Wn.2d 677,
684, 132 P.3d 115 (2006).
Here, having correctly asserted its authority to examine Taxpayer’s records, Audit explicitly
requested Taxpayer’s federal tax returns, banks statements, reseller permits, and other documents
and information—records that Taxpayer was required to keep, preserve, and provide to the
Department. RCW 82.32.070(1). Aside from the single page of a bank statement that had been
provided as part of the audit of an affiliated business, Taxpayer did not provide any of the requested
records or information. Audit determined that Taxpayer had not provided suitable records
sufficient for calculating an actual assessment, and that Audit would have to estimate Taxpayer’s
tax liability. RCW 82.32.070, RCW 82.32.100.
To estimate Taxpayer’s tax liability, Audit attempted to obtain as much information as it could
about Taxpayer’s business activities through a variety of available resources and discovered that
building permits were issued to Taxpayer during the Audit Period and that Taxpayer’s construction
work was noted in a real estate sale listing.
Audit examined the building permits. It noted that aside from the [Address 5] property, Taxpayer
did not appear to own the land where it performed the work, as Taxpayer had not purchased, held
title, or received financing, for such land. Accordingly, Audit properly determined that Taxpayer
performed construction services as a prime contractor.
Prime contractors are subject to retail sales tax and retailing B&O tax, on retail sales of
construction services, unless the sales are otherwise exempt from taxation. RCW 82.04.050(2)(b);
RCW 82.08.020; RCW 82.04.250(1). To calculate an estimate of retail sales tax and retailing B&O
tax, Audit estimated Taxpayer’s retail sales of construction services based upon the limited
information available: building permits and real estate sale listing.
Audit discovered that Taxpayer had been issued four building permits over the four-year Audit
Period – an average of one per year. So, Audit decided to estimate the same amount of retail
construction sales per year, for each year of the Audit Period. Notably, the building permits did
not include the [Address 5] property, so Audit did not include it in determining the average number
of sales per year.
While none of the permits disclosed the value of the construction services, two of the permits
appeared to be for new single family residence construction projects, and the other two were for a

Det. No. 24-0003, 45 WTD 062 (May 5, 2026) 69
new garage/ADU and single-family residence remodel. The only available information that Audit
could find regarding Taxpayer’s construction activities was the [Address 5]. property, which was
purchased for $ . . . and then sold fifteen months later for $ . . . Audit used this limited information
to estimate the gross income from that project to be $ . . . . With four permits being issued over the
four-year Audit Period, Audit estimated Taxpayer’s income based on if it had constructed and sold
one home each year and each such construction resulted in $ . . . in gross income from retail
construction services. Then, Audit assessed the according amounts of retail sales tax, retailing
B&O tax, delinquent penalties, substantial underpayment penalties, and interest, for each year over
the Audit Period.
Taxpayer disputes the estimated assessment and asserts it is inaccurate because it is based on
presumptions and not facts. Taxpayer also asserts that there are no business records for the
Department to review.
As explained above, RCW 82.32.100 affords the Department wide discretion in the methodology
employed to calculate a reasonable estimate of tax. See Det. No. 15-0350, 35 WTD 291 (2015)
(affirming the Department’s authority to assess taxes based on a reasonable estimate and citing
Det. No. 14-0106, 33 WTD 402 (2014); Det. No. 13-0302R, 33 WTD 572 (2014); Det. No. 03-
0279, 23 WTD (2004); and Det. No. 97-134R, 18 WTD 163 (1999)). An abuse of discretion occurs
when a decision rests on untenable grounds or is manifestly unreasonable. Mayer v. Sto Indus.,
Inc., 156 Wn.2d 677, 684, 132 P.3d 115 (2006).
An estimated assessment is an assessment of last resort. The Department always attempts to
calculate an actual assessment based on the facts in taxpayer’s books and records. Though, if a
taxpayer fails to provide books and records, the Department will estimate an assessment based
upon the limited facts available. Here, after Taxpayer declined to provide any business information
or records, Audit used the very limited information available to calculate an estimate of Taxpayer’s
income.
Using the only available purchase and sale prices from one of Taxpayer’s projects, Audit estimated
Taxpayer’s gross income per project to be $ . . . . We find this estimate to be reasonable, and in
Taxpayer’s favor, because the calculated gain from the project is $ . . . ($ . . . sale price less $ . . .
purchase price).
Noting that there were four building permits issued over the four-year Audit Period, Audit assessed
[tax based on] the estimated per-project income of $ . . . for each year. Though more records and
information would have been helpful in calculating an estimate, based on the very limited
information available, we find this estimate to be reasonable. Especially considering that
Taxpayer’s bank statement for one month was four pages long and one page had $ . . . of written
checks. Though perhaps the volume of transactions that month was an outlier, when $ . . . is
multiplied by 12, it produces $ . . . . This would indicate that Taxpayer had income of at least $ . .
. per year to cover those expenses. Further, the volume of transactions in the bank statement seems
to indicate that Taxpayer was performing more than one construction job at a time – in other words,
more than one job per year. Again, we find Audit’s estimate to be reasonable and in Taxpayer’s
favor.

Det. No. 24-0003, 45 WTD 062 (May 5, 2026) 70
Taxpayer also asserts that it does not have any records to provide Audit. That assertion was proven
untrue when Taxpayer provided the single page of its bank statement from December 2020. That
one page proved both that Taxpayer had records available, and that those records would likely
indicate some business activity. Instead of providing any additional bank statements, Taxpayer
continued to assert that it did not have to help Audit’s investigation. Thus, Audit proceeded to
estimate Taxpayer’s tax based on the limited facts it had. Had Taxpayer provided any additional
information, it may have had grounds to question the tax assessed against it. However, Taxpayer
opted to not even provide so much as the additional three pages of the December 2020 bank
statement. With no records provided, Audit proceeded in the manner it deemed best, estimating
Taxpayer’s income and resulting tax based on the sale of one home per year. Accordingly, we
deny the petition as to this issue.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied.
Dated this 4th day of January 2024.

RCW 82.32.090; RCW 82.02.010; WAC 458-20-228 – EVIDENCE OF INTENT
TO EVADE – The Department has the burden of proving a taxpayer’s evasion by
clear, cogent, and convincing evidence. The Department looks to the actions of the
corporate entity as a whole when determining evasion. Failing to remit retail sales
tax creates a prima facie case against the Taxpayer. The taxpayer may then rebut
the Department’s prima facie case.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
for in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
Kelly, T.R.O. – A construction company appeals the assessment of the evasion penalty assessed
after an audit discovered the business collected but did not remit sales tax over several years. It
contends its actions were unintentional. The Department previously denied Taxpayer’s petition.
On reconsideration, Taxpayer provides additional records as to intent and contends the Department
made twenty-three legal errors regarding the evidentiary standard. The new records are insufficient
to alter the determination. We do not find the evidentiary standard was improperly applied
previously. Taxpayer’s petition is denied on reconsideration.1
ISSUES
1. Did the Department properly uphold the evasion penalty under RCW 82.32.090(7) and WAC
458-20-228 (Rule 228)?
2. Does the additional documentation provided by Taxpayer rebut the Department’s prima facie
[case] showing the evasion penalty should apply under Rule 228?
FINDINGS OF FACT
We incorporate the facts set forth in Determination No. 23-0075 by reference and restate only
those relevant to our discussion here.
1
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 49
. . . (Taxpayer) is a construction business focusing on plaster installation [and] based in . . .
Washington. The Department of Revenue’s Audit Division (Audit) audited Taxpayer for the period
of January 1, 2018, through December 31, 2021 (Audit Period).
Taxpayer is a family run business. . . . (Owner) owns the business. Owner hired his daughter . . .
(Daughter) as the bookkeeper in early 2018. Daughter had no prior bookkeeping or accounting
background, having just graduated college with a degree in biology. Pursuant to Taxpayer’s
petition, Daughter’s training consisted of Taxpayer’s prior accountant giving her some instruction
during which, “[Owner] assumed the accountant would address all Washington excise tax
reporting,” and “[Daughter] did not receive the training on excise taxes [Owner] assumed she had.”
According to Taxpayer’s petition, Taxpayer previously, “had some difficulty with reporting,”
where Taxpayer overpaid tax for more than four years. With the help of an outside accountant,
Taxpayer got a refund for four years of overpayment.
Taxpayer’s petition claims that Owner retained control of billing even after Daughter took over
the accounting. He billed customers in Excel with invoices that listed retail sales tax as a distinct
charge. Daughter’s accounting consisted of using Quickbooks, bank statements, customer checks,
and the Department’s website to file taxes, track job costs and profitability, and generally maintain
the books. She used Quickbooks to record expenses and input deposits, but never used it or any
other program for invoicing. Neither Quickbooks nor the bank statements showed sales tax
separately itemized, and Daughter asserts that she did not look at the invoices from Excel showing
sales tax until late 2019. Daughter contends she was unaware that Taxpayer was collecting retail
sales tax from customers. Daughter said, “In summary, there was a separation where my dad would
invoice, and I would submit the taxes.” Taxpayer’s Petition, Exhibit 1, page 1.
During the Audit Period, Taxpayer reported income mainly under the wholesaling B&O tax
classification. Taxpayer only reported under the retailing and retail sales tax classifications once
in November 2021. During the Audit Period, Taxpayer remitted $. . . in retail sales tax. Audit
found sales invoices showing Taxpayer had collected retail sales tax but had not remitted it to the
Department. Taxpayer collected and failed to remit a total of $. . . in retail sales tax during the
Audit Period.
Audit issued a Notice of Balance Due letter . . . on June 14, 2022, for a total of $. . . , comprising
$. . . in tax adjustments, $. . . in penalties, and $. . . in interest to that point.
Audit gave credit on overreported wholesaling B&O tax and asserted retailing B&O and retail
sales tax on sales where retail sales tax was collected but not remitted. Audit also asserted retail
sales tax on wholesale sales due to missing reseller permits. Audit applied a fifty percent evasion
penalty on the retail sales tax Taxpayer collected but did not remit.
Taxpayer timely petitioned for review of the fifty percent evasion penalty. Taxpayer attempts to
rebut the Department’s finding of evasion, contending that the failure to remit retail sales tax was
unintentional. Taxpayer’s petition was denied in Det. No 23-0075. We held that the evasion
penalty was appropriate as Taxpayer knew a tax liability was due, and Taxpayer attempted to avoid
taxation through intentional wrongdoing. We further held that after Taxpayer’s attempt to rebut

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 50
this evidence, the evidence of evasion weighed heavily in favor of upholding the evasion
assessment.
Taxpayer timely filed for reconsideration. On reconsideration, Taxpayer submitted additional
records and argument. Taxpayer provided a number of new records. We summarize them as
additional records demonstrating Daughter’s inexperience in her position, Taxpayer’s transition to
working as a prime contractor in 2018, various bank deposit records, and records of specific
discounts given. Audit reviewed these records thoroughly.
Taxpayer’s additional arguments consist of identifying what Taxpayer terms twenty-three separate
errors in the Department’s determination. In doing so, Taxpayer reinterprets what it believes
should be necessary to prove evasion and terms the application of the current legal standard as
errors. Taxpayer interprets the intent element as applying to individual actors rather than the
Taxpayer itself.
ANALYSIS
The legal requirements for evasion remain the same as in our initial determination. Here we
reanalyze the facts, including the additional information provided on reconsideration, based on the
same law. As such, we reiterate our prior explanation of the laws and rules.
The Department is required to assess a fifty percent penalty if it finds that any deficiency resulted
from an intent to evade a tax. RCW 82.32.090(7). This is further explained by Rule 228,
specifically:
The evasion penalty is imposed when a taxpayer knows a tax liability is due but
attempts to escape detection or payment of the tax liability through deceit, fraud, or
other intentional wrongdoing. An intent to evade does not exist where a deficiency
is the result of an honest mistake, miscommunication, or the lack of knowledge
regarding proper accounting methods. The department has the burden of showing
the existence of an intent to evade a tax liability through clear, cogent and
convincing evidence.
Rule 228(5)(f). We summarize Rule 228 as having two elements. First, that a taxpayer knew a tax
liability was due. Second, that same taxpayer attempts to avoid taxation through intentional
wrongdoing.
The Department has the burden of proving both elements of evasion by clear, cogent, and
convincing evidence. Id. Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence has been described as evidence
convincing the trier of fact that the fact at issue is “highly probable,” or stated another way, the
evidence relied upon must be “clear, positive and unequivocal in [its] implication.” Colonial
Imports, Inc. v. Carlton Northwest, Inc., 121 Wn.2d 726, 735, 853 P.2d 913 (1993).
To meet this burden, the Department must present objective and credible evidence that clearly
demonstrates intent to evade a known tax liability; mere suspicion of intent to evade is not enough
to meet this burden. Det. No. 03-0147, 22 WTD 274, 276 (2003). “Intent is a state of mind. As

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 51
such, it must usually be proved by circumstantial evidence.” State v. LaRue, 5 Wn. App. 299, 306,
487 P.2d 255 (1971). Circumstantial evidence carries the same weight as direct evidence, and
constitutes evidence that allows for reasonable inferences based on common sense and experience.
See State v. Hieb, 107 Wn.2d 97, 111, 727 P.2d 239 (1986). Mere underreporting of collected
retail sales tax does not constitute evasion. Det. No. 98-065, 17 WTD 359, 371 (1998) (evasion
not found where the taxpayer claimed underreporting was due to dishonest bartenders). However,
substantial underreporting of collected retail sales tax does constitute evasion. Det. No. 97-134R,
18 WTD 163, 167 (1999) (evasion found where the taxpayer filed “no business” returns when it
had gross receipts and also failed to remit collected retail sales tax).
Rule 228 lays out a nonexclusive list of taxpayer actions for consideration of intent to evade. The
one example relevant to this analysis is, “The willful failure of a seller to remit retail sales taxes
collected from customers to the department.” Rule 228(5)(f)(ii)(B).
We have previously held that failing to remit retail sales tax creates a prima facie case against the
Taxpayer, stating:
The Board of Tax Appeals has said that in the case of the retail sales tax, a prima
facie showing of fiduciary fraud, and hence a prima facie showing of tax evasion,
is made simply by showing that the seller has collected and failed to turn over the
funds to [the Department]. A seller, as trustee of retail sales tax funds collected
from purchasers, stands in a fiduciary relationship with the state. A trustee owes to
the beneficiary of the trust the highest degree of good faith, diligence, loyalty, and
integrity; a trustee must act solely in the beneficiary's interest. Unexcused failure
to timely turn over trust funds actually collected by a seller on behalf of the state is
a breach of the seller's fiduciary duty, and amounts as a matter of law to fraud on
the state. .
Det. No. 04-0098, 23 WTD 331 (2004) (citing Sunrise Fiberglass Engineering v. Dept. of Revenue,
BTA Docket No. 41913, 13 WTD 203 (1993), and David Grimes v. Dept. of Revenue, BTA Docket
No. 51276 (1998)).
In the same determination we went on to state that the taxpayer may then rebut the Department’s
prima facie case, stating:
Once [the Department] has clearly demonstrated the existence of each of the
elements of evasion, a burden of production is imposed on the taxpayer to come
forward with evidence of honest mistake, ignorance of the law, negligence, or some
other fact which tends to rebut [the Department]’s evidence. Mere subjective and
self-serving statements by the taxpayer regarding intent, without more, are
insufficient to meet this burden of production. Any evidence presented by the
taxpayer must be weighed against that presented by [the Department]. Because the
burden placed on the taxpayer is one of production only, the burden of proof as to
evasion still rests with [the Department]. The evidence of evasion presented by
[the Department] when viewed alone, or along with the taxpayer's evidence, must
weigh heavily in favor of upholding the assessment.

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 52
Id. We also held that business experience tends to undercut or negate the possibility that a taxpayer
was unaware that it was required to report and pay taxes. Id.
1. Did the Department make errors in applying the legal standard to uphold an evasion penalty
under Rule 228?
In the petition for reconsideration, Taxpayer asserts arguments advancing an alternative
evidentiary standard wherein the intent of the individuals working for Taxpayer should be
separately analyzed.
The statute on penalties, including the evasion penalty, applies to “taxpayers.” See RCW
82.32.090. This is further explained by Rule 228, specifically:
The evasion penalty is imposed when a taxpayer knows a tax liability is due but
attempts to escape detection or payment of the tax liability through deceit, fraud, or
other intentional wrongdoing.
Rule 228(5)(f) (emphasis added).
Chapter 82.32 does not define a number of terms including “taxpayer” directly but rather cross
references chapters 82.01 through 82.27 for applicable definitions. In Chapter 82.02 we find a
definition for “taxpayer” which states:
“Taxpayer” includes any individual, group of individuals, corporation, or
association liable for any tax or the collection of any tax hereunder, or who engages
in any business or performs any act for which a tax is imposed by this title.
"Taxpayer" also includes any person liable for any fee or other charge collected by
the department under any provision of law, including registration assessments and
delinquency fees imposed.
RCW 82.02.010. We read this to mean that the liability for the tax is what creates a “taxpayer.”
Neither Owner nor Daughter are primarily personally liable for the tax due by Taxpayer. Taxpayer
is liable for its own taxes. In this circumstance, references to the term “taxpayer” are read to apply
to the corporate entity as it has the primary liability. Thus, when evaluating whether the criteria
for evasion are met, we look at the actions of the tax-paying entity as a whole.
Upon review, we find the Department’s application of the evidentiary standard with the corporate
entity Taxpayer as the “taxpayer” in this circumstance to be consistent with prior interpretation of
rules and statutes. We are not persuaded that there is any legal basis upon which we should grant
the relief requested. We deny the petition as to this issue.
2. Does the additional documentation provided by Taxpayer alter the outcome of the application
of the evasion penalty under Rule 228?

Det. No. 23-0075R, 45 WTD 048 (May 5, 2026) 53
Taxpayer provided a number of new records. We summarize them as additional records
demonstrating Daughter’s inexperience in her position, Taxpayer’s transition to working as a
prime contractor in 2018, various bank deposit records, and records of specific discounts given.
Neither the assorted bank records nor the records of specific discounts given reveal any new
information. Thus, they do not have any impact on the legal analysis of the application of the
evasion penalty.
Both Daughter’s inexperience and Taxpayer’s transition to working as a prime contractor represent
evidence put forth by Taxpayer on reconsideration to rebut the Department’s prima facie showing
of evasion.
Once the Department has clearly established the elements of evasion, a burden of production is
imposed on the taxpayer to produce evidence of honest mistake, miscommunication, ignorance of
law, lack of knowledge, or some other fact that tends to rebut the Department’s evidence. Det. No.
16-0066, 35 WTD 540 (2016). However, mere subjective and self-serving statements by the
taxpayer regarding intent, without more, are insufficient to meet this burden of production. 23
WTD at 338.
Daughter’s inexperience in her position was unquestioned and previously considered. Cumulative
evidence on this topic is unpersuasive.
Taxpayer’s transition to a prime contractor represents lack of experience in collecting retail sales
tax. While Taxpayer previously advanced this argument in its initial petition, it was not explicitly
considered in the prior determination as irrelevant. We reiterate, in this case Taxpayer charged and
then failed to remit sales tax. This is not a circumstance where Taxpayer under collected, remitted
late, or didn’t know it needed to collect tax in the first place. Taxpayer charging, collecting, and
failing to remit over $. . . of retail sales tax over a period of years wholly obviates any suggestion
that inexperience played a role.
We do not find Taxpayer’s new records have any impact on our prior analysis. We sustain the
assessment of the evasion penalty.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied on reconsideration.
Dated this 1st day of September 2023.

WAC 458-61A-215; RCW 82.45.010(3): REAL ESTATE EXCISE TAX –
EXITING TITLE EXCLUSION. The real estate excise tax does not apply to
quitclaim deeds given for the sole purpose of clearing title if no consideration
passes otherwise. In order for their daughter to obtain a mortgage loan to purchase
a property, daughter’s parents went on title of the property, and intended only to act
as co-signers, not as co-purchasers. Daughter later refinanced the property solely in

LaMarche, T.R.O. – Husband and wife . . . who shared title with their daughter on a real estate
parcel that was later transferred to their daughter alone, assert that they were on title only to help
their daughter to get a mortgage, and intended to act solely as co-signors. Grantors assert they are
entitled to a clearing or exiting title exemption from Real Estate Excise Tax (REET) on the transfer.
We grant the petition.1
ISSUE
Under RCW 82.45.010(3)(i) and WAC 458-61A-215, are Grantors exempt from REET on their
transfer of real property to their daughter on the grounds that they merely wished to exit title?

FINDINGS OF FACT
[In May 2018,] . . . (Grantors) co-signed a mortgage with their daughter, . . . (Grantee) and one of
the conditions of the loan was that they be on title on the underlying real property located in
Washington state . . . (Property). County records indicate that prior to the transfer at issue here,
Grantee and Grantors each held a 50 percent interest in the Property.
On March 9, 2019, Grantors filed a REET Affidavit with . . . County for the transfer of their 50
percent interest in the Property to Grantee, and Grantee refinanced the Property in her own name.
No money or other consideration passed between the parties at the time of sale. Grantors claimed
a clearing or exiting exemption under WAC 458-61A-215(2)(e), indicating that their intention was
to go on title simply as “co-signors” only, not as co-purchasers of the Property, and asserted they
had not made any payments toward the downpayment or previous mortgage.
The Department of Revenue’s REET Program audited the transaction. As part of the audit, the
REET Program requested loan documents and other documents related to the transfer, as well as
Grantee’s bank statements from . . . Credit Union. The REET Program found that Grantee’s mother
was on the bank statements and was on the account as a co-owner, and for this reason concluded
that Grantor had contributed to the payments on the Property prior to the transfer. On this basis the
REET Program denied the exemption, and the Department issued an assessment on December 28,
2022, . . . totaling $ . . . , which consisted of $ . . . in REET, $ . . . in penalties, and $ . . . in interest.
Taxpayers timely filed a petition for administrative review.
After filing the petition, Grantor provided a copy of a document entitled “Account Change Card”
for Grantee’s . . . Credit Union account, which indicated Grantee’s mother was not added to the
bank account until September 15, 2019, approximately six months after the transfer at issue.
Grantor also provided copies of bank statements showing Grantee’s mother was not listed on the
bank statement prior to September 15, 2019, and indicating that the down payment and mortgage
payments were made solely from Grantee’s bank account.
ANALYSIS
REET is imposed on each sale of real property in this state. RCW 82.45.060. The term “sale”
includes “any conveyance, grant, assignment, quitclaim, or transfer of the ownership of or title to
real property . . . for a valuable consideration.” RCW 82.45.010(1). “Consideration” includes the
following:
[M]oney or anything of value, either tangible or intangible, paid or delivered, or
contracted to be paid or delivered, including performance of services, in return for
the transfer of real property. The term includes the amount of any lien, mortgage,
contract indebtedness, or other encumbrance, given to secure the purchase price, or
any part thereof, or remaining unpaid on the property at the time of sale. . . .
WAC 458-61A-102(3); see also RCW 82.45.030(3). Certain exclusions exist from the definition
of “sale,” one of which is the transfer of an interest in real property merely to secure a debt. RCW

dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 23-0196, 45 WTD 059 (May 5, 2026) 61
82.45.010(3)(i). WAC 458-61A-215 (REET Rule 215), the Department’s rule that administers this
statutory provision states:
The real estate excise tax does not apply to quitclaim deeds given for the sole
purpose of clearing title if no consideration passes otherwise. This rule does not
apply to deeds executed for the purpose of adding persons to title, except in cases
of persons added to title for co-signing security purposes only.
REET Rule 215(1) (Emphasis added.)
Grantors claimed the exemption example in REET Rule 215(2)(e) on the REET Affidavit, which
states:
(e) The parents described in (d) of this subsection who have been on title with their
child are now issuing a quitclaim deed to Joseph to exit title. Joseph has now paid
off or refinanced the mortgage in his name only. The parents’ intention was to go
on title as “co-signors” only, not as co-purchasers of the property, and they have
not made any payments toward the repayment of the loan. This transfer is exempt
under this rule.2
Here, the date of the transfer was made on March 9, 2019, and Grantor wife was not put onto
Grantee’s bank account until September 15, 2019, thus there was no commingling or joint
ownership of funds as originally believed. No money from the transaction was given to Grantors
(compare Det. No. 19-0037, 40 WTD 137 (2021)), and there is no evidence in the record that
payments were made by Grantors on the original mortgage. Therefore, no consideration passed
between the parties, and Grantors are entitled to the exemption in WAC 458-61A-215 and RCW
82.45.010(3). Accordingly, we grant the petition.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer’s petition is granted.
